Padyā. = Padyāvalī;

Bhakti-rasāmṛta-sindhu;
Mālavikāgnimitra;

Śṛ.ti. = Śṛṅgāra-tilaka;

The Treasury of Jewels of Sublime Sayings.
Homage to the Buddha!
These captivating words of various lords of poets are the supreme ornaments for the throats of the learned.
I shall compose a priceless collection of those great poets' verses that cause the heads [of listeners] to nod in approval. (VidSrk 0.1)

The Sugatas’ arrows— shining with the tips of their crescent-shaped heads raised high, with broad chests armored, full of heat, piercing the hearts of adversaries, and harsh— are [the very ones] that wound.

May that Jina protect you—he whose physical form was beheld by the Māras led by Smara with their garments cast aside, yet neither they nor the breasts of the wives of Māra experienced any agitation. VidSrk_1.1 *(2) //
Of Aśvaghoṣa:
May that Teacher be for your delight—he whose ten toe-nails are bowed down by Brahmā, Śiva, and Kṛṣṇa, those three gods who clearly attained their status as deities through being reflected therein;
he, the preceptor of the three worlds, who has reached the further shore of the ocean of existence so difficult to cross, and who is a valiant hero triumphant over the hosts of Māra. (VidSrk 1.2)
Regarding Vasukalpa:
If it is well known that both desire and anger are adversaries, what indeed was accomplished by the Three-Eyed One through his wrath after killing the Bodiless One?
May that leader of the host of sages, the Kinsman of the Sun, who pacifies a hundred enemies such as Manmatha through forbearance, grant you prosperity. (VidSrk 1.3)

May that Sugata bring about your supreme welfare— he who is the sole bridge for crossing over the shoreless ocean of saṃsāra, and who cannot be swept away by the continuous floods of water at the end of an aeon, even by the forceful pride of the army of Māra’s irresistible retinue. (VidSrk 1.4)
Of Aparājitarakṣita:

May the Lord, the Teacher of the entire world, who has dispelled the darkness [of ignorance], who is comparable to the sun, who shatters the wall of cyclic existence, and who is devoted to crushing the pride of Kāmadeva—the very root of worldly existence—protect us from the lower realms. (VidSrk 1.5)

May those rays from the tips of the toenails of Vasukalpa— the one whose flower is the sprout of the nectar of compassion, whose beauty is the pearl-necklace ornament of his consort Wisdom, and who possesses the rising spray of the river of tranquility— meet upon your heads as various garlands fit for the consecration to the sovereignty of the world, while they shimmer as he moves to bestow fearlessness. (VidSrk 1.6)

May the wish-fulfilling tree of the six superknowledges grant you the fruit of perfect enlightenment—the seed of which is the awakening mind; its trunk is the great height of the mass of generosity, shimmering from the cool, firm watering-trench of meditation cooled by the sprinkling of the water of ethical conduct; its leaves are the broad brilliance of wisdom; its branches are the vigor of unyielding purpose; it bears the blossoming flowers of patience; and it provides a most refreshing shade. (VidSrk 1.7)

These two [verses] belong to Śrīdhara and Nandin. (Skmsa.u.ka. 244) Even though the world was conquered by the side-glances of the women of that one Mind-born God (Kāma), we have sufficiently concealed all manifestations of the sentiment of wonder. But as for the Sugata, who set out to conquer him along with his army, he did not even begin to raise his eyebrows; rather, the mere trembling of his brows sufficed. Thus, the story of his virtues serves us only to cause a paralysis of speech. VidSrk_1.8 *(9)
Of the one whose mind is like a bed of white water-lilies.

Even for the Teacher, who possesses the great superhuman power whose fruit is the desire to abandon the multitude of enjoyers—having taken on a body in every single infinite birth through countless cycles of existence—their enemies praise his excellence; yet what can we say of him [the Buddha] when even Smara, whom he conquered, was instantly reduced to ashes by a mere spark from the fire of the side-glance of Umā’s lover? (VidSrk 1.9) —by Vallaṇa.
May that vow of the Conqueror of Māra protect you—vow which rendered his host of streams [of arrows] barren, wherein he displayed great prowess in opening his mouth to swallow Māra’s head;
for, beholding the reflection of his own wide-gaping maw superimposed upon Māra’s joined palms, the excellent warrior Māra’s composure was utterly overturned. (VidSrk 1.10)
May the handful of blossoms—possessing the unprecedented beauty of flowers formed by the fresh, thick hue of pollen as they meet with the playful swaying of their own feet moving restlessly in sport;
and which are made to bloom wide by the loud mutual kisses of swarms of bees greedy for honey that embrace them—bestow upon you the highest welfare when offered to one’s own beloved.

May that Teacher bestow upon you happiness and auspiciousness—he who delights in having conquered his enemies; whose teeth, possessing a luster intensified by the rays emitted from the sequence of his throbbing, crimson lower lip as it is released in a smile, pervade the space before him; and who, like the dense glow of twilight rising at the end of the night of ignorance, possesses a majesty that brings about its cessation. (VidSrk 1.12)

May the Jina protect you—he who was praised by Rati with tears, trembling, and horripilation: by her whose passion overflowed with mature longing because his form was more beautiful than even Kandarpa’s; by her whose heart was agitated with fear because he had brought old age upon the most excellent of women; and by her who bowed low with a weight of devotion because his heart was impenetrable even by the arrows of Māra. (VidSrk 1.13)
"Of him alone," says the scripture:

May the Śākya Sage protect you—he whose method of worshipping with blue lotuses is made manifest by the multitude of eyes shimmering on the golden body of Indra, who has fallen prostrate near his lotus feet; and he whose unprecedented saffron robe is revealed by the sprouts of radiance rising from the crowns of the gods who bow down to him. (VidSrk 1.14) (15)

"O you who are like Vasu, who are you alone, O flower-armed one, in the act of destroying my meditative concentration? Even if all the gods were armed with flowers, what of it?"—may that Teacher, the conqueror of the Māras of the ten directions, who surely reduced them here to the state of having flowers as weapons, grant you his weapon. (VidSrk 1.15)
Thus ends the section on the Sugata. //1//

2. May that lotus-handed one protect you—he whose stainless face possesses a weight of dense beauty and fragrance such that neither the lotus nor the moon can rival it; he who, with a rain of vast sheets of moonlight as pure as the splendor of Lokeśvara, brings sleepless joy to the bees and bears the wonder of unrestrained delight for the cakora birds. VidSrk_2.1 *(17)

Victorious is the Lord of the World, whose face possesses the splendor of a mass of white rays; his gaze is moistened by innate and profound compassion, and he has quenched the thirst of the entire host of pretas with a flood of nectar flowing from the lotus-hand that grants boons—[the work] of Buddhākaragupta. (VidSrk 2.2) (18)

May Lokeśvara protect you—he who resembles a mass of snow upon the waves of the Milk Ocean churned by Mount Mandara as it revolves with its dense roar and steady form driven by an exceedingly violent current; he who is encircled on the glorious Potalaka mountain, which resounds with the echoes of profound commentaries, by the splendor of his own dense mass of light rays. (VidSrk 2.3)
From the nectar-filled lake of your heart, made lush by the rain of compassion, a stream has issued forth—charming in its gradual attenuation through the channel of mercy.

It has become fivefold as it flows toward the slightly parted lips of those afflicted by thirst via various conduits of movement; what else could this be but the five fingers of your hand? (VidSrk 2.4)

I bow to the Lord who possesses three eyes—he who, like the sun, bears infinite light; who, like a poet, has his hymns composed by a multitude of gods; who, like spring, is filled with compassion; and who, like the moon, is the protector that moves through the sky. (VidSrk 2.5)

If this smallness of the belly of Puruṣottama were not innate to it, but rather to his heart, how could there be such indolence in his own interest? How could there be such pursuit of others, while his mind is set on doing what is beneficial? (VidSrk 2.6)
"His face is not this storehouse of digits;

this whiteness is not the brilliant moonlight; his eyes possess the luster of water, yet the moon has no pair of spots despite its intense radiance"—having inferred this, the lotus approached the presence of the Moon, smiling fearlessly. May that face of the Lord of the World, which truly is such a lotus, be for your auspicious day! (VidSrk 2.7)
Like the new sun within a mass of matted locks, surrounded by dark clouds, Amitābha gazes upon a cluster of red Aśoka blossoms;
may he—who appears as if his form were fashioned from the luster of the moon—shatter your weariness and bestow upon you waves of the nectar of tranquil bliss. (VidSrk 2.8 [24])
These two belong to the Buddha-family—thus ends the section on Lokeśvara. 2.

3. Thereafter, let Mañjuśrī be remembered—whose beauty is like a cluster of blooming blue lotuses strung together by the shimmering thread of his crest-mark, garlanded by swarms of bees falling toward the rays of light overflowing with the fragrance of his limbs;
whose form is bristling with the garlands of rays radiating upward from the tips of his toenails, as if worshipped by showers of flower-clusters released by the gods. (VidSrk 3.1) [25]

May Kumāra protect the world—he whose dancing Bhairava-self is like the mass of smoke from the fire flashing from his body as he raises his sword, resembling the conflagration at the end of an aeon; who is like a swarm of flies upon the head of the Mahiṣa demon offered to the infinite universe between his horns; whose multitude of feet is sluggish with compassion for the gods, who have spread their own feathers out of fear and abandoned them; and who has eclipsed the sun with the flood of his stars. These two [verses] are by Vallaṇa.

May the Youth who upholds the lineage of the Sugatas protect you for a long time—he who was gazed upon in various ways by the celestial nymphs: with sound by the one bearing a sword, with thought by the one bearing a book, with sport by the child, and with longing by the most beautiful maiden. (VidSrk 3.3)

May that Mañjuvajra be vigilant for your welfare and happiness— he who, with the saffron-red water of splendor poured from the golden jars of the lotus-feet of the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), whose sprout-like fingers are charming, consecrates one who pays homage in the kingdom of Dharma. VidSrk_3.4 *(28)

"Of these whose feet have conquered their enemies, and who possess the splendor created by the beauty of Mañjuśrī’s lovely face—where indeed have we even heard their names? Yet, this blue lotus moves with audacity near me! May this pair of eyes of yours, reddened at the corners as if out of anger, protect you. (VidSrk 3.5)
Thus ends the section on Mañjughoṣa. //3//

4. Then follows the section on Maheśvara: Victorious is that God who bears the trident as his weapon, by whom the three worlds were fashioned as his craft, whose poetry is the triple Veda, who brought about the destruction of Tripura, and upon whose head the triple-pathed river (Gaṅgā) acts as a garland; he who carries three blazing eyes, as if to behold the three times, and who is the delimitation of the three qualities (*traiguṇya*). VidSrk_4.1 *(30)*.

[This is] the work of Vasukalpadatta. Victorious is the exhaustion at the limit of aiming by the Foe of Cities (Śiva), whose arrow was launched from a bow drawn by the power of the preeminent serpents as they bowed and rose; while the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa), exhausted by the sparks of the momentary fire of his wings as he rushed on in the hope of supporting the Ancient Puruṣa who had become his speech, was still sleeping. Vidyaśrīkara 4.2 *(31)

May the moon protect you—he who is the sprout of jewels for the head-garland of Maheśvara; he who, bitten by the leader of the serpent-host eager with the savor of the longing to drink the flowing nectar, was held and squeezed in a pair of tongs to fill his orb, and is now being drawn out by the flames from the crest of the eye on Śiva’s forehead. (VidSrk 4.3)
"O digit of the moon, may there be welfare! O river of the gods, may there be auspiciousness! O row of skulls, may there be prosperity! O serpent-king's vine, may there be well-being!

O mass of matted hair, may there be safety for the universe!"—may that Tandava dance of the actor who plays the role of the Destroyer at the end of the aeon bring you fortune, wherein these [deities] gather and speak thus to one another when he has attained tranquility. (VidSrk 4.4)
"O Goddess, behold! As these lotuses, the friends that rival your face, gradually turn red in the sky, this state of affairs occurs.

May the twilight worship of Śambhu protect you—worship in which his hands were joined in *añjali* under the pretext of imitating the closing lotuses, thereby deceiving Pārvatī who was accustomed to such a ritual. (VidSrk 4.5)
By Rājaśekhara:

"O Pārvatī, why are you so harsh? This is the innate nature of those born of the mountains. Why are you devoid of affection? Ashes are rough to the touch; they do not disparage affection anywhere. Your anger toward me is fruitless; what fruit could there be from such behavior directed at Sthāṇu, my beloved? May Śambhu, thus rendered speechless by his beloved, bring you prosperity. (VidSrk 4.6)

O Enemy of Tripura, from the manifestation of Bhojadeva’s body, I inferred that in a previous birth I likely never bowed to you anywhere. Now, bowing in this life, I am already emaciated and shall not be able to endure much more in the future; O Great Lord, may these two offenses of mine be forgiven. (VidSrk 4.7)

What need is there to speak of the greatness of the great ocean, that mountain which, terrified by the strike of Indra’s thunderbolt, sank into the mass of waters like a tiny reed-boat? Even Maināka, wallowing in the deep waters, found rest within the hollows of the walls of a hut made of the tips of moss-sprouts tossed up from the backs of pāṭhīna fish. (VidSrk 4.8)

Salutations to that Śambhu, at whose armlet the serpent Śeṣa reached— a Śeṣa who, by taking refuge in the expansive jewel of his hood, assumed the form of a horizontal mark [on the moon], while this earth, sealed by seven such oceans and surrounded on all sides by as many sky-scraping mountains and vast continents, [rests upon him]. (VidSrk 4.9)

May the rows of severed heads of corpses, strung upon the stalks of serpents, protect you—those heads whose ghostly state has been dispelled by the essence of nectar melting from the moon, which is scorched by the flames of the poison-fire issuing from the broad hoods of snakes whose throats are distended with tightly knotted swellings; and which repeatedly gaze with wide-open eyes, tawny with the luster of their pupils, out of a thirst for blood. (Vallana’s verse, Skmsa.u.ka. 13) VidSrk_4.10 *(39)
Vallaṇa’s (attributed to Bhavabhūti):
His hair, beard, and eyebrows were tawny like the peak of a mountain engulfed in a forest fire; with his three eyes, fierce and tawny-pupiled, he was like a dark cloud pierced by three suns.

May the southern face of Śambhu destroy your evil—his face which reveals the very depths of the Pātāla through the radiance of his moon-like fangs, and which strikes terror into the three well-formed faces [of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva]. (VidSrk 4.11) By Rakṣovibhīṣaṇa:
May he protect you—he who blocks the mass of darkness with the moonlight of his half-moon, which is made to blossom by the brilliance of his unrestrained teeth.
May the loud laughter of Śambhu, who has begun his dance, bestow blessings upon you—a laugh possessing the deep resonance of a row of rain clouds.

May the head of Dhūrjaṭi protect you—the head upon which the mass of matted locks is tawny, fierce, and loosened by the lord of serpents as he slips from exhaustion under the weight of the onset of a violent dance; a mass where the Gaṅgā flows with shimmering waves, where crescents of the moon rise, where rows of falling skulls resound with a swelling whirring noise from the intense gusts of wind circling within them. (From the *Śaṅkhamitrasūkti*, verse 37) (Vidvatsabhārañjanī, verse 4.13 [42])

May Śambhu himself, who became elevenfold when accompanied by the ten reflections of his own image reflected in the mirrors of Gaurī’s nails as she bowed at his feet— may he be victorious! (Vīryamitra) VidSrk_4.14 *(43)

May the matted locks of the Lord of Beings protect you—locks entwined with the coils of serpent-creepers, their topknots bound by garlands; wherein the Mandākinī falls in scattered streams amidst the mass of skulls fixed as crests, their radiance mingled with the light from the sockets of his forehead-eye that is like lightning, and where the lovely moons are obscured by the tips of tender ketaka flowers. VidSrk_4.15 (44)
From Bhavabhūti (*Mālavikāgnimitra*, Act 1, verse 1):
Victorious is that mass of Ganges water resting upon the lofty crest of Śambhu, wherein the digit of the moon sinks and rises again like a minnow. (VidSrk 4.16 [45])

May that moon protect you—curved like the tip of a fresh lotus stalk, which shines placed upon the fire-tawny head of the Enemy of Smara (Śiva), appearing like a crystal-white sprout emerging from the skull-bowl as it is moistened daily by the flowing waters of the Mandākinī. (VidSrk 4.17)
Of someone [Rājaśekhara]:
Having formed a circle with a digit of the moon that had fallen and a bracelet broken during a lovers' quarrel, the Daughter of the Mountain, her face beaming with laughter—
May that Śiva protect you whom she beholds, and may that Daughter of the Mountain protect you, and may that Moon of Play protect you—he whose digits are filled by the rays of his teeth. (VidŚrk 4.18)
By Vararuci:
Homage to the one who is beautiful with the moon-knobbed chowrie kissing his lofty head.
To Śambhu, the foundational pillar for the construction of the city of the three worlds.

May that fire of Śambhu’s arrow burn away your misfortunes—that arrow which, like a lover who has committed a fresh offense, was cast aside by the young women of Tripura as they clung to his hand; which, though violently struck, seized the hem of her garment; which, when grasping her hair, was brushed away; which, when it fell at her feet, was not even looked upon in the confusion; and which, when it embraced her, was shaken off by those whose lotus-eyes were filled with tears. (Bāṇa) VidSrk_4.20 *(49)
May the gale-winds protect you—those winds of Bhīma, who is addicted to the grand display of his twilight *tāṇḍava* dance, and whose circular arms, whirling with fierce speed, sweep across the earth;
for when these winds rose up with such velocity that the mountain ranges seemed to fly away instantly, Indra beheld once more his thunderbolt. (VidSrk 4.21)

May the fire vomited from the corners of the eyes of the three-eyed Śiva— blazing with radiant splendor as it first flickers among the hair, crackles intensely upon the skin, grows faint in the flesh, emits *ṣṭhātkṛta* sounds amidst the flowing blood,
and suddenly flares up with great beauty in the marrow-filled parts of the limbs— dispel all misfortune. (VidSrk 4.22)

May that Dhūrjaṭi protect you—he at whose performance of the *tāṇḍava* dance during the full-moon twilight, the golden mountain [Meru], shimmering like a forest, was tossed about along with the moon by the swaying of his armlets and necklaces;
and who, with his lovely luster, his trembling locks of hair, and his earrings, bears the splendor of the head of the Earth when she is shaken by the most wondrous amazement.

Deep in the hollow of the skull, thin within the joints of the matted locks, and surging against the cluster of jewels on the hoods of the crest-serpents—may the long, resonant murmur of the Gaṅgā on Śiva’s head, soft at the corner of the crescent moon as it trembles by the force of its current, purify us. (VidSrk 4.24 [53])

(From Skmsa.u.ka. 46, by Yogeśvara) May the garland of skulls of the Lord of the worlds be for your peace—a garland whose script, with its not-very-well-known syllables, the Gaṇas read word by word here and there:

"He will create the universe; he will protect the earth; he will rule over the waters; he will be taught by the Nāgas; he will take delight among those possessed of passion; he will destroy the world; and he will enjoy the heavens. (VidSrk 4.25) *(54)

May the mass of matted hair of Śambhu protect you—tawny with the rays of the young sun, dwelling together with the moon whose body is as delicate as a fresh lotus stalk; it is like a flame rising upward from the ripened fire of his ascetic heat, like the beauty of an anthill where snakes dwell amidst the high waves of the Gaṅgā, and like the twilight that accompanies the moon. (Bhojadeva’s *Śṛṅgāraprakāśa*, verse 61) VidSrk_4.26 *(55)*.

Salutations to you, the destroyer of the afflictions of the world and the remover of the three cities, who—though the daughter of the mountain fled in terror, she could not abandon you because she was pursued by the ever-spreading southern half [of your body]; and who, though your foot rose swiftly toward the crown of his head, did not cause the destruction of the established order of the heavenly realm, for which the assembly of the best of gods rejoiced and offered praise. (Skmsa.u.ka. 56, by Ravināga) VidSrk_4.27 *(56)

May the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of Śambhu protect you—his absorption which is joined to Brahman through a dissolution occurring at the moment of emptiness; he whose knees are encircled by the double-folded coils of the serpent in the *paryaṅka* posture, whose senses are restrained by meditation having ceased due to the internal suppression of breath, and who beholds the Self within the Self alone, free from the instruments of perception, through the vision of reality. (Bāṇa’s *Śrīkaṇṭhastava*, verse 11)

May the dance of the Lord who bears the crescent moon on his crest protect you—his great firebrand-wheel formed by the hosts of Rudras, Arka, and Tārās whirling with the force of the wind-like revolutions of his incessant arms; a dance from which flows the Ganges cascade, beautiful with the light of eyes issuing from the rays of the moon flashing from his towering crown that strikes against all the mountains as it bends, rises, and slithers like fire. "Mother, what is this that Father has hidden in the hollow of his joined palms? Is it life? "My child, it is a sweet fruit; he will not give it to me. Go and take it yourself. May the outburst of laughter protect you—that laughter which, when Guha had thus sent away his mother, forcibly drew apart Śambhu’s joined palms in the *añjali* gesture, its impetuosity checked by his broken meditative absorption.
Of the Lord of Yoga:
"O fair-browed one, place your creeper-like arm thus; take this stance; do not bend too far forward; keep your toes slightly curled; look at me for a moment!
May the clapping rhythms of Śambhu, who causes Gaurī to dance with his own face as a drum sounding like a rain-cloud, bringing forth the pauses in the tempo, grant you happiness. (VidSrk 4.31) *60*
Of that very [fire]:

Victorious is the Lord whose eyes are moist with compassion, who—having beheld the smoke-bannered fire flickering among the sprout-like silken garments, steady among the strands of braided hair, slow among the seams of bodices, and possessing blazing flames upon the slopes of the breasts of the women in the harem of Tripura—let go his bow from his hand. (VidSrk 4.32)

(Śkmsa.u.ka. 73) When Śambhu kisses the lotus-face of the Daughter of the Mountain, the moon enters the thicket of his matted locks, the lord of serpents descends from his shoulder with his hood gracefully curved, and the bull, feigning deceit, scratches his eye with the tip of his hoof. VidSrk_4.33 *(62) //

May the cloud upon Śiva’s head—turbulent with the currents of the triple-pathed river (Gaṅgā) gushing forth with various velocities; terrifying due to the unseasonable heat from the eye in his forehead as it whirls rapidly; and emitting sounds released by the impact of the wind moving through the hollows of the rows of skulls; like the onset of the rainy season—be for your welfare. (VidSrk 4.34) [63]
May he protect the universe even today— he upon whose head the new moon does not wax,
as if out of shame at being eclipsed by the face of Gaurī. (VidSrk 4.35)

May Hara protect you— he who was looked upon by Pārvatī with shame when she saw him as "Dig-vāsas" (the sky-clad one), with a charming smile when he was called "Manasija-dveṣin" (the hater of the god of love), with wonder that "this is Viṣamekṣaṇa" (the odd-eyed one), with fear at the thought "Kapālī" (the skull-bearer), with envy because "he has taken the Jāhnavī (Gaṅgā) upon his crest," and with trepidation because "he wears bracelets of serpents. VidSrk_4.36 *(65) //

May the mutual anxiety of Hara and Guha to protect one another when the god of the Vinaya (Śiva) is enraged by the serpent and the peacock, and when the peacock is distressed by being encircled by his [the serpent’s] body, protect you all. (VidSrk 4.37)
May the fire born from the discharge of the arrow of the Destroyer of Tripura destroy your misfortunes—

the fire that brings the splendor of vermilion to the foreheads, golden liquid for the ear-ornaments on the temples, the red tint of betel to the faces, saffron unguents upon the jars of their broad breasts,
and the beauty of lac-dyed silk garments upon the hips of the wives of the lords of the Daityas as they flee while Jātārdhavardhana is born.

May Hara protect you— he who is embarrassed by the clamor of the celestial nymphs, terrified by the fear that the circle of the sky was being submerged by the fierce waves born from the seven oceans, as they surged upward due to the wind from the hissing of the serpent-king’s hoods, which were agitated by the force of his mass of matted locks whirling in the current of the waters of the divine Gaṅgā. (VidSrk 4.39) (Maṅgala 77)
In the presence of Karkarāja (the son of Brahmā),
the lord of the gods bows low; terrified by the fear of the emerald crest-jewel [of Viṣṇu], the serpent-king Mañjīka retreats.

May the Enemy of Tripura protect you—he who, while adjusting his slipping lower garment, wears the deerskin, and whose range of vision is met by the smiling side-glances of the Daughter of the Mountain.

May that Śaṅkara protect you—he who, though adorned with the *śakti*, bears the moon, the daughter of Śrīśaila, and the celestial river; he who is skilled in the policy of the King of Wonders, even when the mouthful of fierce *kālakūṭa* poison has been digested, when the God of Love has been forcibly burnt, and when the fire at the end of the aeon has assumed the thinness of his radiant forehead-eye. (VidSrk 4.41)

"The Goddess has given birth to a son! Dance, O Gaṇas! Why do you stand still?"—when Bhṛṅgiriṭi was thus embraced by Cāmuṇḍā, who spoke these words with uplifted arms out of joy, may the sound produced by their skeletons rattling within their cages as they moved against one another protect you—a sound that surpassed the deep resonance of the drums being beaten. VidSrk_5.1 *(71) //
May the pair of breasts of the Lord of Yogins— belonging to Him who dwells on the mountain and which resemble the frontal globes of Indra’s elephant— protect you.
[The body] of Dakṣa, smeared with the ash-body-paste resulting from the pressure of Śaṅkara’s firm embrace of his neck;

[the world] whose stability depends on the fragments of the cosmic egg splitting apart due to the trembling of the tortoise whose shell is bent down by the crushing of the earth-globe as it reels in the agitation caused by the forceful Niśumbha.

I salute your playful sport, which cast the seven oceans into the cavities of the cheeks of the underworld’s rival wrestlers, and which manifested its supernatural power before the assembly of Nīlakaṇṭha’s delighted followers. VidSrk_5.3 (73)
"O guardians of the quarters, move aside! O clouds, leave the sky! O Pātāla, depart! O Earth, enter deep into the interior of the ground!

(From Skmsa.u.ka. 93 by Yogeśvara; Smvsū.mu. 2.30) "How is there such sweat on you, O dearest? O Lord, why does this trembling come from the fire of your eyes? May the assembly at Śambhu’s descent into dance purify you—an assembly where Ambikā lowers the fresh garland from her lotus-face hanging down to her knees; where Nandin arranges the crescent moon in its proper place and binds his matted locks with the lord of serpents; where Kāla ties his hide, and Kālarātri brings a skull-bowl into his hand. "O Bhṛṅgin, release the horn! O Gajavaktra, let go of the base of the tail! O Nandin, you have little joy; O weak Mahākāla, enough with this clutching of the neck!

Having spoken thus, may the bull bring you happiness as he is led to the feet of Pārvatī, watching with his eyes the Three-eyed Lord who looks embarrassed, his neck turned and his dewlap quivering. (VidSrk 5.7)
To Abhinanda:
O Bhāgīrathī, salutations be to you, who are doubled in depth on the head of Hara, which is crowded by Gaurī’s half being divided! (VidSrk 5.8)
This is that Bhāgīrathī, the crest-ornament of the blessed Bharga, who flows from the ocean toward the abode of the lotus-born god;

having abandoned her body here, she swiftly carries people to the world of Brahmā by means of a current of most intense velocity, even those who have turned against the flow. (VidSrk 5.9) [Smvsū.mu. 1.24] (Skmsa.u.ka. 49)

Seeing her husband’s lip stained with the collyrium from the night before, and the finger-prints of ash upon the bud-like breasts of their daughter-in-law, the young wives, smiling sweetly out of the joy of love, whispered something, something indescribable into the ear of Gaurī’s mother. May she be victorious! (Vidagdhamukhamandana 5.10)

May those nails of Śubhāṅga protect the universe— those nails which, from their tips, wash away the lac-dye from the peaks of [Mount Kailāsa], which bear garlands of *mālatī* flowers upon the circle of matted locks, and which, with their upward-surging pure rays, eclipse the moon when the Goddess falls at the feet of Śiva. (VidSrk 5.11)
O Gaurī, while the God Dakṣa—who bears your creeper-like body in close embrace—may indeed experience an intense joy born from incessant hugging;
yet the heart of the Three-eyed Lord suffers repeatedly, for he does not see that gaze of yours, so steady with love, sweet, tender, and charming. (VidSrk 5.12)

May the leader of the dancing hosts of Gaṇas protect you—he who, as he dances, imitates the elephants of the quarters whirling upward as they are tossed by the earth shaking from the impact of Bali’s footsteps;
and whose trunk-tips, when raised high, repeatedly draw in and release the circle of stars, making them practice the playful sport of scattered spray. (Skmsa.u.ka. 139) VidSrk_5.13 *(83) //

May the head-shakings of Gaṇeśa protect you for a long time—those head-shakings, accompanied by the trumpeting of bees flying from his temples, which resounded through the quarters as the Lord with the Trident performed his dance; when the Lord of Serpents, recoiling his coils in terror of the peacock of Kumāra summoned by the sound of the drum struck by Nandin’s hand, entered the cavity of his nostrils. (VidSrk 5.14)
From Bhavabhūti (*Mālatīmādhava* 1.2):
"Where has that mother and father gone, who formed this pair into a single body; and where, moreover, have those two halves gone? Let the noble one tell us."
Victorious is the elephant-faced son of the Fire-god, who brings about the realization that this entire world has arisen as consisting of nothing but men and women.

May she—the supporting staff for those drowning in the waters of the ocean of existence, the thunderbolt-edge for the mountain that is the great asura Mahiṣa, and the royal swan upon the lake of Hara’s heart—grant long-lasting auspiciousness to the world. (VidSrk 5.16) By Bhagīratha. (Skmsa.u.ka. 108)
Victorious is Gaurī, whose lower garment is stained with the blood of the buffalo-demon Mahiṣāsura struck by the trident given by Bhagīratha;
she appears bashful like a woman in her menses when looked upon by Hara as he smiles. (VidSrk 5.17)

May that handful of flowers offered by Gaurī protect you— she who, during the auspicious wedding rites of Gonanda when the ceremony was imminent, saw before her the form of the bridegroom Śiva himself depicted [on the wall], and who, after a long time and with great difficulty, placed the offering at the feet of her beloved according to the words of an old woman, while overcome by confusion, laughter, anger, and shame. (VidSrk 5.18)
Bhāsa’s: (Skmsa.u.ka.
112, Spdśā.pa. 102, Smvsū.mu.
2.37) The Lord of Birds, having performed an exceedingly difficult feat, desires to lie between his parents.

"Those two also share a single body"—thus the uneven dice triumphs for a long time. "This is my mother; this is not my mother, for she does not have a coarse, brownish beard on half her face. This is my father; this is not my father, for I have never seen a breast here upon my father's chest.
Who is she? Who is he? What is this—is it a young woman, or a man? Could it be a third gender? May Guha, who turns away in apprehension upon seeing the form of Śambhu, protect you all.

May Guha protect you from calamity—he who, having rolled at his father’s will upon the breast of the funeral pyre until his limbs were covered with the dust of the ashes, suddenly plunged from the mass of Śiva’s matted locks into the fathomless waters of the Gaṅgā; he who immediately utters cries of "sīt" from the coldness of the water, his row of teeth chattering, trembling as he places his hand over the eye [of Śiva] that blazes with the flame of fire.
By Bāṇa. (VidSrk 5.21; Skmsa.u.ka. 146; Smvsū.mu. 2.43)

May the six-faced one, who rests upon his father’s lap and is intent on the play of childhood, protect you—he who, out of curiosity for a flight of swans, wears a row of skull-ornaments; who, with impetuosity for a lotus stalk, swings a young crescent moon with his hand; and who, mistaking it for a red lotus, opens his eyes wide toward his forehead.

May Heramba, bearing an exceedingly beautiful splendor like that of a moving peacock-feather parasol—due to the swarms of bees that have flown up from the temples of Balabhadra, trembling under the influence of fear yet clinging in clusters above out of greed for the ichor of rut—accomplish the destruction of the world's evils without hindrance. (Skmsa.u.ka. 149) VidSrk_5.23 *(93) //
(ŚKMSA.U.KA.
142) May that One alone protect the worlds, emulating the conduct of Gaurī and the Lord of the Mountain;
he who, though possessing but one tusk, shines as if he has yielded his wife by giving up half his body—the portion of his face where teeth are absent. VidSrk_5.24 *(94) //

May the childhood utterances of Śaktidhara bring you auspiciousness—utterances which, while he tore open the flaming cavities of Vāsuki’s mouths and touched his sprout-like fangs as he counted with his forefinger the poison-spotted snakes that hissed, were an erratic sequence of numbers: one, three, nine, eight, seven, and six. (Skmsa.u.ka. 141, by Vasukalpa) VidSrk_5.25 *(95) //

May the laughter of Kumāra protect you—he who, having fashioned a peacock before him with its head nestled within the folds of its wings while it slept, was crying out from childhood, "Father, who cut off its head? How did this happen?"; and whose heart leaped at the clashing of his two hands as he brandished the Pināka bow in secret laughter, finding satisfaction in gazing upon that very head. (VidSrk 5.26)
(ŚKMSA.U.KA.

148) "How does he always protect this fierce lion from the inquiry regarding the garland of human skulls, the bull, the serpents, and even his son the peacock?"—pondering thus within himself upon the long-standing skill of the Lord's intellect, Kūṣmāṇḍa daily nourishes the splendor of his belly, which is filled with steadfastness. (VidSrk 5.27) [*(97)]*

"Father, why have you come from home? Tell me, what is the news there? Has the God been defeated by the Goddess?"—as the Lord of Peacocks thus spoke, [listing] the bull, the *ḍamaru* drum, the funeral ashes, the lord of serpents, and the moon, may the sudden cry of Bhṛṅgirīṭi, born of the agitation caused by the loss of his master’s alms and ornaments, long protect the world. (VidSrk 5.28)
"This one is fat; he will not go far. This one is thin; he is not capable of traveling. Therefore, it appears that the acquisition of food there will belong solely to me, the one remaining."

May that mutual hostility between Bhṛṅgin and Kūṣmāṇḍa, which was contemplated again and again at the beginning [of the wedding] when Lord Śiva and Śivā were taking each other's hands in marriage, protect you. (VidSrk 5.29)

May the side-glance of Ambikā protect you—a glance that bears the grace of a bee wandering about out of longing for her ear-ornament of blossoming sprouts, and which is entwined by the mass of rays from the nails of her hand as it flickers behind the *khaṭakāmukha* gesture fixed by the drawing of the bowstring. (Skmsa.u.ka. 156) VidSrk_5.30 *(100) //

"Mother, that humiliation you suffered from the Kāpālika due to his biting of your lip—let it be recounted to Brahmā and the others," as Guha spoke these words repeatedly, Gaurī, seeing herself unable to stop the six-faced one’s speech with her two hands, turned away fruitlessly toward the four-faced Brahmā out of embarrassment; may she protect you for a long time. (VidSrk 5.31)

May the Daughter of the Mountain protect you—she who, at the time of her marriage, was both joyful and afraid; she who, for a certain snake, had separated the medicinal dust from its body; for a serpent, held herbs in her hand; for the potent poison held in her palm, wore a gem upon her neck; and for the multitude of spirits of her husband, recited the syllables of the mantra taught by her aged maternal grandmother. (VidSrk 5.32)

By Rājaśekhara. (Skmsa.u.ka. 111) "If he is naked, what need has he for a bow? If he possesses weapons, what need has he for ashes? If his body is smeared with ashes, why does he have a woman? And if she is there, why does she loathe desire? Seeing this behavior of his own master, which is so full of mutual contradictions, Bhṛṅgī maintains a body that is nothing but bones, harsh and bound with thick veins. (VidSrk 5.33) [103]
(Skmsa.u.ka. 151, by Yogeśvara) // Thus ends the section on the hosts of Śiva’s attendants //5//
6. Next follows the *Harivrajyā*:

The Lord, the Master of the entire universe, who bears upon his chest the mark of the leaf-design from the breasts of Śrī, and who is the rising moon to the lotus-faces of the wives of Madhu—under him, when he assumed the body of a boar for sport, the earth shone like a single grain of *mustā* grass dug up from the bed of the puddle that was the ocean of dissolution. (VidSrk 6.1) [104]

May the breaths of the Lord in the form of a tortoise— sleeping due to the scratching of the tips of the rocks of Mount Mandara as it circles behind him with great force— protect you; [these breaths belong to] Vākpatirāja (or Nagna).

Due to the power of following the traces of past impressions (*saṃskāra*), the unimpeded coming and going of the waters of the ocean through the shifting of the tides does not rest even today. (VidSrk 6.2)

We worship without hindrance the two radiant eyes of the Blessed One, who bears the mace Kaumodakī as his mark— eyes that are expert in delighting the cakora birds and providing them with their feast.
By means of these two, the lotus bud in the pond of his navel—possessing a sweet beauty charming with half-awakened sleep and lulled by half-drowsiness—was made a rival to the conch shell.

Salutations to that treasure-house of the universe, whose belly the self-born Brahmā entered in order to see its foundation, its nature, and its arrangement— Brahmā, who at every moment ceases his activity during the great aeon (*mahākalpa*) and whose sole dwelling is the path of the navel, acting as the architect for the city of the three worlds. (VidSrk 6.4)
These two belong to Murāri:
"O Rādhā, you are angry; you alone are angry. You are the mother of the earth, for you alone are the mother of the worlds; there is no other who is wise."
"O Goddess, in this playful quarrel of our amorous sport, you alone are infinite"—smiling thus, Śauri bowed to the beautiful cowherd girl; may he bring you prosperity. (VidSrk 6.5)
Of Vākpatirāja: (Skmsa.u.ka. 276; Pvpadyā..
284) "Who is this Hari at the door? Go to the grove. "What is there with a monkey? "I am Kṛṣṇa, my dear. "I am terrified. "But how can I, who am Kṛṣṇa, be a monkey?"
"O simple one, I am Madhusūdana; go to that very creeper with its flower-nectar. May Hari, thus rendered speechless by his beloved and filled with shame, protect you. VidSrk_6.6 (109)
Of Śubhaṅkara:
When the day was fading, he returned the herd of cows while his flute played in a low, sweet tone; he wore a crest of peacock feathers upon his head, grey with the dust raised by the cattle.
May Keśava grant you blessings—he who, though weary, possesses a charming form encircled by a withered forest garland, and who is a festival for the eyes of the cowherd women.
Of someone:
Out of reverence, for the sake of fulfilling Viṣṇu’s desire to crush the hosts of Dānavas, he was grasped with the palms of his two hands and marked with a row of fingernails by Śrī.
May Śaṅkha—emerged from the mouth of his lord who dwells within the ocean’s belly, as if surrounded by a succession of progeny—purify your blessings. (VidSrk 6.8)
Victorious is that primordial Boar, who crushed the great mountain like a kaseru root with his tusk,
before whom the elephants of the gods became like sprouting mung beans.
May those drops of ocean water prevail, which, rising from the lashing of the tail of the Lord in the form of a fish, made the surface of the sky appear as if adorned with a hundred moons.

By those [flames] which, turning back as they fell, made the body of the fire Aurva—tangled with its mass of flames—the long-time abode of the pain of indigestion through the force of being swollen by their consumption. *VidSrk* 6.10 (113).

"Whence do you come? You are but an atom. What is 'your own' by its own nature? Why do you not desire anything belonging to anyone? Do you truly want three steps, or what with this trivial bit of earth?
"The three worlds are mine"—such was the intention of Hari, which, though concealed, triumphs as it is revealed through these indirect utterances of the peaceful Brahmin.

"May prosperity long attend her; may she not be obstructed by the flanks of Mount Mandara with its great waves, nor even by the venomous saliva of the Lord of Serpents!"—may that speech of Hari protect you, which, while he gazed at the Goddess Śrī as she half-emerged from the ocean, vibrated within his throat and was manifested outwardly through his facial distortions, thus revealing his inner intent. (VidSrk 6.12)

May the fire born from the friction of the saw-like claws of Hari as he strikes the chest of the lord of the enemies of the gods purify you— that fire which crackles "caṭat-caṭat" upon the skin, hisses "ccham" as blood spurts forth, crackles "dhagat-dhagat" in the fat, and blazes most intensely "ṣṭhāt" upon the bones. (VidSrk 6.13)
These two belong to the Lord of Speech:
(Skmsa.u.ka. 197; Spdśā.pa. 126, Smvsū.mu.
2.77) I praise [the one] whose complexion is sprinkled with droplets of milk from the Ocean of Milk, which was churned by Mount Mandara whirled by his arms.
The chest of Murāri, which rivals the sky variegated with stars, is a lake of blooming white water-lilies.
Of Murāri:
The king of mountains wanders upon his back, the ocean roars near his ears, and the poison-fire with its spreading lattice of flames burns the worlds;
yet the Blessed Lord Kūrma sleeps between the two halves of the cosmic shell, his neck resting at ease, his eyes languid with the weight of slumber. (VidSrk 6.15)

May either the eyes or the body of Hari bring about the pacification of the suffering of existence for you—those eyes which are fond of being gazed upon by those prostrate in devotion, which rival the blue lotus, and which are led by those intent on meditative absorption to serve as the object of their meditation for the attainment of the ultimate good; or that body which, as a great treasury of loveliness, extends the capacity for aesthetic delight to the eyes of Lakṣmī. (VidSrk 6.16)

May Hari in the form of the Fish protect you—he who, when the ocean spread out as it was tossed by his tail, summoned the ancient sage Agastya with a longing for a confluence with the celestial Gaṅgā;
while he drew forth the Vedas from the vast resonance of the essence of the syllable *Oṃ*, there arose in the sky a pillar consisting of water and ether in the midst of the sea.
[And may he protect you]—he whose eyes were wide open in a yawn, and who longed to fondle the lotus-hand of Lakṣmī, who had first awakened...
May the unimpeded feigned sleep of Murajit protect you—sleep which left only the remainder of his body diminished by the weight of its own contraction.
O friend, that rogue was sought by me throughout the entire night, thinking "he might be here," "he might be there," as he skillfully went to meet another woman;
yet the enemy of Mura was not seen at Bhāṇḍīra on the riverbank, nor on Mount Govardhana, nor on the shore of the Kālindī, nor in the grove of *nicula* trees.
"Śyāmoccandrā sleeps; O child, sleep does not come to me, Mother. "O son, listen to a story for the sake of sleep; tell me one that is unprecedented.
"It is clear that Narasiṃha emerged from a pillar, intending to tear asunder the Dānava"—at these words, a smile arises on the face of the Son of Devakī.
Of Śatānanda:
(Skmsa.u.ka. 257; Pk 151 Sarvānanda;

BRK 5.1761) With the Kaustubha jewel throbbing upon a chest whose joints are loosened as the knots of its muscles are released, and with the deep sound of the *Sāman* chants emerging from the cottage of the bud-like lotus of his navel;
May the body of Murāri protect you—its wondrous majesty increasing with every step—as it was gazed upon with joy by Bali, who was eager to obtain the vessel.

May the body of Lakṣmī purify you—her body which, as she rose at the end of their dalliance, rested one hand upon the lord of serpents for support and held her garment with the other, while her shoulder bore the weight of her loosened tresses; and which was then drawn back to the bed by Śauri, his love for the sexual union doubled by the beauty of that very moment, his arms languid yet radiant. (Vākpatirāja, Skmsa.u.ka. 220) VidSrk_6.22 *(125)

2.33, Vs 1.3; Skmsa.u.ka. 339, Svsu.ā. 79, Spdśā.pa. 135).
The moon rises again in full splendor with its rays; then this pair of frontal globes of the elephant appears; and then this shimmering cluster of blossoms atop the celestial tree.
May that Goddess Lakṣmī—who was thus mistaken for the curved line of hair on the face, the two breasts, and the belly of the churning Ocean of Milk by the gods—be for your welfare.
May the wielder of the plow (Balarāma), speaking with words faltering from intoxication as he sat in his drinking vessel, bring you prosperity— "Bha-bha!
The earth is reeling; la-la-la! The moon is falling; kṛ-kṛṣṇa! Speak quickly, Ha-ha! Are the Vṛṣṇis laughing?
Si-sīdhu! Mu-mu! Release me! Pa-pa-pa! (Vidagdhamukhamandana 6.24)

"O Puruṣottama-deva! What, what is this? O Lion! Then what is it? O Lord, is it a body resembling a human? It is a marvel! It has not been captured. Is that so? O Jīva, bring him here quickly! Surely he has already arrived."
"Bow after bow, but no sword—oh, the swiftness and the hardness of my claws! May he who thus struck the king of the Daityas with his own claws like thunderbolts protect you.
—Of Śrī Vyāsāpāda (Skmsa.u.ka. 200, Smvsū.mu. 2.76).

May the Enemy of Mura protect you—he who, assuming the form of a playful cowherd, has taken up the sport of tending cattle; he whose single leg is encircled by a staff, his arms resting upon his head as he sings songs of bull-fights, his crest-jewel fashioned from a tethering rope, and his long-standing passion fixed upon the delight of the combat between two great bulls bristling with pride. *Śrī-Sonokka* (Vidagdha-mukhamandana 6.26).
Victorious are the sprout-like claws of Hari in his form as Narasiṃha, which have torn open the chest of the Daitya;
reflecting upon whose deeds, the enemies of the gods tremble even before the nails of their own beloveds during sexual union. (VidSrk 6.27) *(130)

"O Lakṣmaṇa, these clouds distress me who am separated from Jānakī; and these cruel breezes from the Kadamba trees strike my very vitals. May Hari, who was thus beheld with jealous suspicion by Rādhā as he spoke of his separation in a previous birth while dreaming, bring you happiness. (VidSrk 6.28)
Of Śubhaṅka:
(KK 2.69[70]; Skmsa.u.ka. 263, Pvpadyā.

252) Those [mountains] upon which Garuḍa was born with his neck turned away due to the false scratching [of the serpents], and which were neither noticed nor heard by the hoods of the bed-serpents as they feigned sleep;

May those amorous dalliances of Mādhava protect you—dalliances that mock the goddess Lakṣmī, which were never even glimpsed by the Creator through his eyes, half-closed in the guise of a continuous meditation.
(From Rājaśekhara, *Śṛṅgāraprakāśa*, verse 6.29; Skmsa.u.ka. 338):

Her gaze sluggish from the fresh awakening [of passion], momentarily averted from the light of the jewel-lamps, she makes her own movements heavy with yawning that produces droplets of water through the breaking of her limbs.

May the squinting gaze of Hari protect you—his eyes long reddened by the interruption of sleep as he desired to cast off his serpent-body from his bed, using the circle of its broad hoods as a pillow.
From Viśākhadatta:

He did not find relief for the itching of his shoulders by crushing mountain peaks with his fangs; nor did he obtain a bath for his limbs in the oceans, for the water was scanty, entering only into the hollows of his hooves.

Victory to that Boar, whose desire was unimpeded by his sovereign power, who— having reached the mire of the netherworld (pātāla)— did not indulge in wallowing, but rather employed only his snout for the lifting of the earth; [this verse is attributed to Vākpatirāja,
though it appears in Varāhamihira’s *Śiśupālavadha* commentary].
May that Blessed Keśava, the playful fish, protect the three worlds—he whose flanks have bruised the circles of the quarters as he rubbed against them, and whose belly is as vast as many oceans;
by the curiosity of his leaping, the vessel of the universe, studded with the bristling hairs on his hard back, has somehow been worn out upon his limbs. (VidSrk 6.32)
