VidSrk_10.5 *(219)*

How were those nights spent by those away from home—nights when gentle winds blew at the end of the showers, when the sky was veiled by clouds, when the quarters of the horizon were glimpsed for a moment during flashes of lightning, and when the moon, stars, and planets lay dormant;

nights that bore the fragrance of nectar-like Kadamba blossoms drenched by rain, and where the croaking of frogs spread unchecked due to the absence of travelers? *Vidvatsamvādaślokasaṃgraha* 10.6 (220).

The riverbanks—resounding with the cries of water-fowls, where cobras slumber upon the tips of reeds, where geese call out, where herds of deer have formed their dung-heaps, and where the waters overflow; banks now overspread by greedy cranes whose matted plumage is gathered by swarms of ants, and filled with wild cocks—make the mind of the Lord of Yoga (or of someone) restless today. (VidSrk 10.7) [221]

Having called his beloved—who was lingering somewhere nearby—with sweet warbling notes, and then, after glancing toward the various quarters of the sky, having left the stage-like ground with his feet;
this peacock now dances joyfully, accompanied by the sounds of clouds as sweet as the resonance of a large drum, while a canopy is fashioned for him from his rows of tail feathers. (VidSrk 10.8)

The clouds, drenched with yellow water, pour forth their waters in continuous streams; sleep comes upon the eyes that are closed by the sound of those torrents. When the people in every house have become silent with eyes sealed by sleep, the nights become filled with clamor by the loud, discordant croaking of frogs. (VidSrk 10.9)
Awakened by the sound of falling raindrops, the cries of the *dātyūha* birds in their cages mingle with the warbling from their throats;
in the watchtowers where the spray is kept back by reed-curtains, the fortunate men drink the lotus-like faces of their wives. (VidSrk 10.10)

The mountain ranges are now free from forest fires; the ten directions are bristling with the sprouts of clouds over forests that have burned and regrown; the sky is released from the dust of the earth; and furthermore, the kadamba flowers have acquired the luster of a woman’s face blooming with the swelling waves of the *kalikā* bud. In how many moments are the knots of the peacocks’ vow of silence severed? (VidSrk 10.11)

In a field where the bellies of the young rice plants are filled with fresh water and the frogs croak slightly, while the ground along the edges of the banks is as white as heaps of conch shells, children with sticks in their hands—smeared with streaks of mud—run about impetuously in every direction, shouting "Cubhru! Cubhru!", eager to catch the leaping fish.
With the space between them suffused by the radiance of shimmering sapphire gems on all sides, this cloud is like a blue silk parasol for Indra who has descended to the mortal world. (VidSrk 10.13)

With masses of darkness streaked by fireflies, with clearly flashing lightning, and manifesting the swelling of great clouds through their smooth rumbling; with trumpeting elephants and vāraṇa-musk deer, and with the preceding winds scented by various *ketaka* flowers—these nights, with their falling rain, I cannot imagine how people separated from their lovers will endure them. (VidSrk 10.14)
When the rain-cloud has arrived, swollen with its own roar and drenched in intoxication, it bestows a restless lethargy upon the mind;

as it thunders, I imagine even the sky itself falls asleep, resting its lap against the quarters of the horizon and making them resound with the roars of water-bearing clouds, its eyes—the sun and moon—seemingly sealed shut. (VidSrk 10.15)

During the rainy season, under the deep rumbling of clouds as they pour down incessant torrents of water, the fortunate men— whose eyes are slightly heavy with sleep, who have climbed onto the roofs of sturdy houses where their barren wives are like pumpkins, and whose chests are pressed by the weight of their lovers' breasts— listen at night while embracing their women with both arms in the leafy thickets. (VidSrk 10.16)
"With the dust and its transformations gone, the light of the stars obscured by thick layers of clouds,
and bearing the weight of hanging breasts— this rainy season is like an aged woman.
"Enveloped within by the flickering flames of the submarine fire of the ocean, these turbid waters were clearly drunk out of thirst by those who, through delusion, mistook it for the sea."

Ah, how else could the clouds be burning, appearing as if with the guise of flames in the form of a shimmering circle of Indra’s bow, while possessing the luster of charcoal that is half-soiled? (VidSrk 10.18)

By making the path slippery and thus obstructing her progress, by drenching her cheeks with thick droplets of water and thereby erasing the decorative patterns upon them, and by repeatedly flashing with the play of lightning to point out the way to the house of her lover—the cloud has rendered assistance to that unchaste woman by swiftly providing atonement for its offense. (VidSrk 10.19)

When the rain has ceased, do the nights—thick with deep darkness—emit these flickering rows of fireflies that fall everywhere like the dust of lightning flashes violently ground by the collision of masses of rain clouds? They touch the minds of travelers' wives with the suspicion of being a continuous shower of sparks from the fire of love. Vidagdhamukhamandana 10.20 (234)

Making the sky seem as if it could be reached by hand, making the quarters of the world appear as if they were dwarfed, shattering the thick clouds in an instant with their roars, and raising a tumultuous sound of raindrops—where indeed is there any dry land that is not submerged? For at night the clouds pour down, while the entire earth is watched by the elephants with eyes wide open in the form of fierce lightning flashes. (VidSrk 10.21)

With their wings drooping and shaken, their tails tucked in, and making whirring sounds as they wheel about, the peacocks dance with their beaks open and feet repeatedly lifted in the cadence of the rhythm; with their necks raised high, their plumage-brushes meeting near their upturned throats, they gaze at the dark cloud-streaked sky that resembles their own necks. VidSrk_10.22 *(236) //
Now enough of these bamboo groves, which are friends to the mountain forests, rivers, and villages, and which have become companions to the unrestrained secret trysts of Śabara couples;
their bases are encircled by the sheaths of young shoots whose tips are like the ears of a young goat dark with bristling hair. (VidSrk 10.23)

With their eyes closed, their heads resting on their wings, and having gradually submerged themselves, these birds—afflicted by the heat—now find relief in the fresh water; repeatedly touching their shoulders, backs, and chests along with the root of the wings, they remain with their knees drawn up, while droplets of water rise rapidly as they vigorously flap their wing-cavities.

Even the marrow is moistened by the raincloud for one who has not performed meritorious deeds—[the cloud] that offers the firm embrace of a young elephant eager for the sport of emerging [from the water].
(VidSrk 10.25) His cries are like the thunders; his tears are like the ocean of unceasing torrents; and the fires of grief arising from their separation are equal to the flickering of lightning.
My beloved’s face is within me, and the moon is yours; our condition is thus the same. O friend cloud, why then are you constantly intent on burning me?
Of Yaśodharman (Smv-sū-mu.
43.33): "Do these [streams] spring from the earth toward heaven, or do they descend from heaven to the surface of the earth?
Are they moving or still?"—pondering thus, the women touch the streams with the tips of their fingers. (VidSrk 10.27) (241)

With his body confined within a crystal cage by the weight of the streams of pure water flowing from the hanging umbrella, the traveler was led away as if he were a beloved woman being carried off by the command of Kama, provoked to anger by her husband’s transgression of their own teachings. (VidSrk 10.28)
Today water will fall everywhere upon the earth; today its heat shall be quenched; today the countryside, eager for the harvest, will strive in the fields.
O cloud, at your rising today, the peacocks—sportive and languid in every direction, their crests covered by the parasols of their swaying tails and plumage—will dance.
The blue-throated one sings, and Gaurī dances with eyes as flickering as lightning;
thereafter, this great Kāla, the rain-cloud, beats the drum. Upon her tresses there is the luster of powdered incense, and on the surface of her cheeks, the appearance of drops of perspiration.

The one who has achieved his purpose beholds the water droplets of those curious clouds fresh from the rain. (VidSrk 10.31) "O fickle one, you cannot remain [here] when the time for the clouds to fall has come;
you are longing. "No, no, my friend! The path is indeed slippery. (VidSrk 10.32)
The fresh *ketakī* flower, entwined by a young, dark serpent,
shines like the fallen tusk of an elephant encircled by an iron ring. Today, upon the stalks of the *ketakī*, the leaves appear increasingly stunted.
The needles [of the thorn-apple] burst open, their filaments having the hue of the woolly tails of young rams.

(VidSrk 10.34) With his limbs smeared all over by the pollen of *ketakī* flowers, with dark clouds for his hair bound upon his head like a skull-crown (*kapāla*) with rows of cranes quivering within, and bearing a curved staff (*khaṭvāṅga*) made of a fragment of a rainbow beautiful with its array of banners of flickering lightning—this Kāla-Kāpālika has arrived, striking terror into women whose husbands are away. (VidSrk 10.35)

O traveler, how can you sustain your life while dwelling in such a rainy season—a time when the quarters of the sky are dark with clouds, the rainbow has appeared, the brilliance of lightning plays, day and night are shrouded, the thundering fills the mind, the playful anger [of the peacocks] has faded, the streams are full, the thirst of the *cātaka* birds is stilled, and the luster of the moon is bewildered? (VidSrk 10.36)

Having forcibly shortened the nights, having violently seized the waters of the rivers, having scorched the earth, and having utterly destroyed the thickets of forest trees—where has the hot-rayed sun gone now? Thus intent on searching for him, the clouds seem to roam in every direction with the light of lightning-lamps. (VidSrk 10.37)
Of someone (according to Skmsa.u.ka. 1287, oṅkaṇṭha; according to Spdśā.pa. 3869 and Smvsū.mu. 61.18, both attributed to Pāṇini).

With masses of darkness terrifying from the flashes of lightning, with the sky obstructed by the dense barriers of incessant black clouds so that the luminaries are banished, and with trees near the edges where glow-worms have risen up, these nights—surpassed only by the humming of swarms of insects intoxicated by the rainwater—cultivate a profound depth. (VidSrk 10.38)
O Abhinanda (or of someone), these mountain expanses have become like flowering young trees in the forests, their broad plumages of beautiful eye-spots made radiant with joy;
they are touched by serpents emerging from their hollows with half their bodies visible to drink the wind from the clouds, appearing like the tips of bamboo shoots sprouting forth. (VidSrk 10.39)
Of Śatānanda:

These riverbanks of the marshlands, where clusters of *nalada* grass grow upon muddy shores, where conchs resound and shoals of crabs sport, and whose waters are turbid with floating seaweed; where the ground is pitted by the mounds of mud vomited up by burrowing earthworms with their protruding heads—these banks produce a pang in the heart. (VidSrk 10.40)
Upon this fresh, essential downpour of the Lord of Yoga, the Supreme Lord, there flows the path of the saphara fish— white as cowries, playful with joy, and resting upon the dry land.
With their hands occupied as if counting the crabs wandering about, these marshy lands, displaying their manifest wealth, seem to be selling their very hearts.
The rain-bearing cloud,
acting with righteousness, now bathes the great linga of Mount Vindhya with pure waters released from hundreds of jars that are like sapphire clouds. (VidSrk 10.42)
In the cauldron of the sky, the great cat that is the cloud now drinks the milk of moonlight, its tongue being the flickering streaks of lightning. These two [verses] are by Yogeśvara.

With her half-emerged womb-cavity, which is soft and copper-colored like the palm of a plantain tree, she drinks the torrential rain—feverish from the summer heat—as if with the hollow of her cupped hands. —By him (the same author): VidSrk_10.44*(258)/*tasyaiva*—
With streaks of water flowing down to the very ground like climbing creepers, the sky appears like a banyan tree, its dark foliage shining with the luster of rain clouds. (VidSrk 10.45)
With her hips made tawny by girdles fashioned from *nīpa* flowers, her shoulders adorned with *kandalī* buds resting upon her ears,
and the area around her breasts pale with *yūthikā* garlands worn as necklaces— such was the natural and lovely attire of the beloveds of Dakṣa’s daughters. (VidSrk 10.46)
When the black collyrium has been wiped away by droplets of rain, when the fine dark garment covering the jar-like breasts has become indistinguishable from them,

and when her natural, slender beauty is revealed— blessed is the fortunate man who, having achieved his purpose, stands waiting as those wanton women of the rainy season prepare their various costumes.

The moon is nowhere to be seen as if it does not exist, and the sun is as if gone abroad; the circle of planets and stars in the sky is as if erased after being drawn. Day or night—both have lost their distinction—due to clouds gathered in dense masses; what is this terrible resolve? (VidSrk 10.48)
For someone [else], speech has been employed, hope for life has been fixed in the mind, and travelers on the road have cast their hopes upon their feet—

only so long as these foothills of the Vindhya mountains, filled with dark clouds that possess the luster of snakes freed from their sloughs and where the *dhārākadamba* trees are in bloom, have not yet been beheld. (VidSrk 10.49)

At the will of the Lord of Yoga, (Skmsa.u.ka. 911) the cranes—whose world consists of devouring fresh locusts—plunge into the rows of young grass on the banks of rivers, near the mountain slopes and close to the nests of buffalo herds.

In a certain corner of a field, a flock of pigeons somehow pecks at the grains of *kodrava* millet, their efforts hindered by the fear of a scarecrow made of grass and wild plants placed within [the grain]. VidSrk_10.50 *(264)
These two belong to the Lord of Yoga:

when that cloud has gathered, having practiced several *kakāra*s that produce a *repha* twice as long as the final syllable, that ruddy sheldrake with its moving, broad throat moves forward, rising in pitch by degrees and becoming slow and sweet through the process of descending. (VidSrk 10.51)
Thus ends the "Wandering during the Rainy Season. //10//
11. Then followed the autumnal excursion:
Autumn, bearing Indra’s bow upon her pale cloud-breasts like the marks of fresh nail-scratches, and propitiating the spotted moon, increased the heat of the sun even further. VidSrk_11.1 (266)
"O moon-faced one, though I possess the splendor of a cloudless sky and lips as lovely as the blossoms of the bandūka flower, shame on me!
For this autumn seems to carry a great heat, as it were, because my ample breasts have withered away. (VidSrk 11.2)

These autumn days are a delight to the mind (Manovinoda): they are hospitable to the swans, the very elixirs that restore life to the lotuses whose lifespans have been consumed by time; they are the rejuvenation for the clouds. In these days, the rivers—variegated by the arrival of wagtails and with their inner sandbanks rippling ever so slightly as the waters recede—draw the heart away. (Vidagdhamukhamandana 11.3)
With their smoky-grey wings and pale bellies flitting about on all sides, the *khañjana* birds scatter the approaching autumn like women scattering parched grain with haste;
and the moon-faced night, smiling, places upon the stage of the sky a jar-like moon, white from being drenched in nectar, accompanied by its auspicious sprout-like spot.
In the sky, rows of white-winged swans cast the shadow of white clouds; and upon the water, by means of their hundreds of reflections, they create the illusion of white lotuses.

If it were not for these autumn waves—sweet with the sound of jeweled anklets, loud and smooth—which moisten the heart with longing through their tinkling, where else would the mind find such delight? (VidSrk 11.5)

With their garden trees made to bristle with joy by the dense, tall blossoms of the *śephālī* flowers that embrace the earth closely at their hearts, the dwellings of the night bring delight; they are filled with the impetuous songs of joyful *kurara* birds, while the quarters of the sky are drenched with the fragrance of blooming water-lilies shaken by the wind. (VidSrk 11.6)

Upon the ground of the circles of night-lotus blossoms, as the dust settles, these young men—muttering some high mantra of the God of Love with loud *huṃ* sounds—are now overcome by the defeat of their persistent pride;
meanwhile, the thick, honey-intoxicated clamor of the master-bees swells forth.
Looking downward with its head turned and tilted to both sides, moving slowly in a smooth circular path through the sky due to the steadiness of its wings, the hawk—
expert in its prey— after a long time, swooping down with extreme lateral speed, suddenly strikes with its moving talons and head.
With its tail held high, its feet moving with playful grace, and its long, dangling wings fluttering; its beak made slightly vocal by a throat resonant with the sweet, intoxicated warbling of joy;
the *khañjarīṭa* bird dances for a while near his beloved, whose eyes are fixed upon it with longing and moistened by waves of tears of happiness. (VidSrk 11.9)
These [scenes] delight the mind:

the banks of autumnal rivers, white with the luster of rows of herons bowing down at their tips as they are occupied by the pursuit of schools of fish submerged within the water; where wagtails wander about; whose surroundings are covered by rows of warbling *kādambara* ducks; and where lines of *kurabaka* shrubs hum sweetly with intoxication. (VidSrk 11.10)
The sun shines fiercely like a low-born man newly enriched; the ruru deer sheds its horn like an ungrateful friend;
the water becomes clear like a sage’s reflection on the Dharma; and the mud dries up like a poor man consumed by passion. (VidSrk 11.11)
Of Bhāsa (Skmsa.u.ka. 1313, Svsu.ā.
1821, Spdśā.pa. 3907, Smvsū.mu. 62.3)

Scorching with the heat of her sighs, speaking in a voice like that of a swan, wearing garments as white as the abode of frost, and bearing breasts that are pale and full—this autumn shines forth like some young woman separated from her lover. (VidSrk 11.12)

With their intentions gradually stilled, the ten directions flow like long rivers from the sky at night— bearing banks of sand from the fragments of the moon’s white orb, strewn before them with flocks of cranes warbling sweetly, and covered by the blossoming water-lilies of the stars in diverse forms.

With their hindquarters broad and expansive due to full, distended thighs, the herd of white cows wanders through the outskirts of the villages—lands green with newly sprouted crops—during nights smiling with the intense radiance of the moon, while the heavy bells, jingling deeply from the weight of thick, dangling dewlaps, fill the air. *Vidagdhamukhamandana* 11.14. (279)

Upon its back, which has the luster of a fragment of conch shell, marked with rows of leaf-patterns red as lac-dye, the *kumuda* flower—its outer petals tawny and green like *gorocanā*—fragrantly blooms in the water of the pond. (VidSrk 11.15)

These forest rivers, with their waters as clear as glass and dark blue as sapphire, inspire terror: their currents are rendered treacherous by the obstruction of thick, massive reeds; their entry points are suspicious due to the sand on the banks churned up by the bellies of crocodiles that have emerged and turned back; and their muddy depths reveal fresh, moist impressions marked by the distinct tracks of tigers.
The tracks of carts are now merely the essence of crushed sugarcane rinds, with the dust-flags stilled; flocks of parrots settle upon the heads of the *śūkāla* rice, bowed low by the ripening grain.

From the fields, rows of minnows enter the reservoirs through the irrigation channels; the clear mud on the riverbanks brings comfort to the ox-driver as he rests from the heat of the sun. (VidSrk 11.17)
Abhinanda’s:

The sprouts, though marked with mud, possess a luster like that of one who has just bathed and anointed herself; the marshy banks, filled with tufts of *kāśa* grass driven by the wind, resemble flocks of rams. The rivers, with *khañjana* birds hastening to settle upon their freshly formed banks, appear as if their eyes were smeared with collyrium; and the swans, against the backdrop of the sky which bears the brilliance of Kṛṣṇa’s body, carry the beauty of conch shells. (Vidvadbhaṇitasaṃgraha 11.18)
Those lotus-root bulbs, which, when swallowed by cooing swans, produce a certain deep, gurgling sound through their rolling in their acidulous throats—
those very bulbs, now rivaling the tender sprouts of the tusks of young female elephants, have emerged from the beds of lotuses.
The wild boars now turn toward the boundaries to seize the handfuls of ripening rice; the trees have had platforms constructed for them by their owners;
the pigeons have built dense nests in the branches for the sake of their young; and the anthills have their inner soil dug out by jackals with their sharp claws. (VidSrk 11.20)

With Indra’s cotton-wool, tossed by the wind—soft as a digit of the moon, resembling streams of saliva from the celestial elephants, and serving as the laughter of the quarters of space, which creates the illusion of green foam from chariots exhausted on the road—the curious maidens are well able to fashion playful ear-ornaments. (Śatānanda, Skmsa.u.ka. 1312; VidSrk 11.21 [286])
The necklace’s luster rests between the breasts of this fair-limbed girl; Acyuta serves as the earring-stem with fresh blue lotuses at the edge of her ears;
and that radiance which was once provided by red gems in her parting is now supplied by bandhujīva flowers—thus the seasonal attire of the rice-guardian bestows a supreme splendor. (VidSrk 11.22)
To Madhuśīla—

today the rivers bring joy, their branches clearly visible as they recede from afar, their banks frequented by wandering wagtails, adorned with royal swans sporting vigorously, and their waters smiling with minnows darting about in fear of being swallowed by the beaks of wandering ruddy geese. (VidSrk 11.23)

The banks of forest rivers, where the forests have emerged and are shimmering, where successions of waves lie upon drying sandbanks, where only the water in the hollows remains, and where the mud is marked by the footprints of swans— these captivate the mind of the childlike. (VidSrk 11.24)

The forest groves on the banks of rivers, their hollows emptied of water by the crushing of female serpents and their branches hung with dead moss and sprouts, now recede far away, yet they proclaim the greatness of the river's former flow. (VidSrk 11.25)
For Śubhāṅga, the days have ripened—their vital energy spent, fragrant with the scent of the ripening palmyra fruit;
they are difficult for the twice-born to endure, as their heat has been quenched by the invitation to the ancestral feast. (VidSrk 11.26)
For the lord of yogins—there is the receipt of funeral offerings from the wealthy and the slippery path leading to his dwelling;
these two things disturb the minds of the twice-born residing in the military camp. (VidSrk 11.27)
Of Vāgura—thus ends the "Wanderings in Autumn" (Śarad-vrajyā). 11.
12. Then follows the journey of winter:
the friend of the frosty winds, the sign of the kunda flowers, the messenger of death for the lotus ponds;
where women, distressed by numbness under the pretext of sleep even while their lovers' thoughts are intense, cherish a firm embrace of their beloveds. (VidSrk 12.1)

Whose mind is not now made eager by the clusters of betel-nut trees, beautiful with fruits that are marked with dark spots like *tilaka* ornaments at their tips; which are as pink as ripe *paṭola* gourds in their middle due to the intensity of ripening; which are slightly brownish at their base; and which are thick and as green as the feathers of a parrot at the stalk? (VidSrk 12.2)
At the bases of the petals, the pollen of the filaments—once fallen and now motionless—no longer carries away the brilliance of yellow orpiment;
within the bud of the night-lily, bees of dull luster lick the nectar mixed with frost at dawn, making it taste increasingly bitter.

The morning breeze blows freely, fragrant with blooming priyaṅgu flowers and scattering concealed sparks of fire under the guise of frosty mist over the lotus ponds; it is capable of stabilizing the horripilation on the cheeks of the florist’s wife, which is swelling with the intense joy of witnessing the abundance of kunda blossoms. (VidSrk 12.4)

The peasants take pride in being praised by hundreds of travelers regarding their straw; the thick vapors from the night-long rumination of the pregnant cows bring comfort to the cowherds. At dawn, with the first rays of the sun sinking into his back, the great bull lies at the edge of the village boundary, his eyelashes moist with frost and covered by a bed of mustard flowers. — By Yogeśvara (Kavīndravacanasamuccaya 1327).
The groves of *damanaka* shrubs, once pungent and sweet with their fragrances and displaying leaf-patterns carved into their foliage,
are now entirely pale with their stalks.
[In this season,] one might rest upon a new bed of *kalama* rice straw with a pillow on a corner of a field, within a light grass hut.
The frost, marked with lines by the great heat from the jars of their breasts, avoids from afar the sleeping couple of plowmen. (Vidvadbhañjikā 12.7)
Of Bhavabhūti (Drda.rū. 4.22, Svsu.ā.
Having observed a pair of rabbits fleeing from the edge of the field, these peasants— having summoned others and raised a great clamor with excessive zeal—
abandon their desire to reap the rice and run hither and thither, both old and young alike, with sickles, ropes, and cudgels held in their hands. (VidSrk 12.8)
Having placed her patched garment behind her back, she sits between her two thighs—which are marked by the scars of burns from fire—resting her hands upon the fire of chaff;

covering her sides, numb with trembling, with both elbows, her skin bristling with horripilation, this old woman does not leave the interior of the house today, neither in the morning nor in the evening. (VidSrk 12.9)
For the Vaiśya—
may the fire of dried cow-dung, consisting mostly of smoke, its brilliance repeatedly vomited forth by constant agitation, and being perpetually tended by the season,
shine as it is enjoyed at the close of day by the women of the cowherd stations, who have cast aside their playful garments from around their breasts with the tossing of their arms. (VidSrk 12.10)

Now, at the close of day, these villages—intent on their labors, with the outskirts sprouting with harvested rice from the threshing floors, and girdled by circles of smoke from cow-dung fires glowing with the weight of ash—captivate the heart. (VidSrk 12.11)
At the base of Abhinanda’s [tree], the jujube fruits are green; at the sides, they are yellow; and at the tips, they are red.
Now, these sweet and fragrant jujubes have reached a state where they are not yet fully ripe. (VidSrk 12.12)
"May you be blessed! It is fitting that your fame is proclaimed by hundreds of travelers; it is only right that your form is unsurpassed, for by your virtuous generosity, Karṇa has been surpassed.
Having observed this for a long time with a pitiful gaze, the plowman—praised by a traveler who had come from afar and who delighted in a mere handful of straw—now wallows in pride. (VidSrk 12.13)
Of the Lord of Yoga (Yogeśvara).
Thus ends the section on Winter (Hemanta-vrajyā).
13. Then follows the section on the Cold Season (Śiśira-vrajyā):
Even regarding the Kunda flower, people do not show such devoted interest in its ritual worship, nor in their own adornment, nor even in the preparation of gifts as they do in [the following].

Just as women delight the minds of young men at the inaugural consecration of the Kunda-caturthikā festival with their "ulūlu" cries and soft, sweet sounds, so too do they gratify the god of love when he is summoned. *VidSrk* 13.1 (306)

In the forest of *damanaka* shrubs, smoke-grey from the fires of dried cow-dung, the falling frost—clinging to the hair—makes the houses of woven cloth difficult to discern; it displays a perverse grace, concealing the appearance of the sun while now bestowing a whiteness over the entire bodies of travelers. (VidSrk 13.2)
Pūṣan, the traveler of the sky, has set out from the eastern mountain at dawn, his body draped in a collar of dense mists that can be pierced only by a needle;
I think that because he was embraced by fire all night long, he is unable to quickly hasten his feet, which remain bound by their sluggishness.

At dawn, the channels of mountain torrents—though far above and level with the sky—seem to the traveler’s startled gaze like full pools of water, emitting thin streams of vapor from their waters and causing even a momentary slowing of his pace. (VidSrk 13.4)

The jests of lovers separated from their wives regarding the mines of *kairava* flowers, and their playful longings for the production of water upon their own beloved stones bathed in frost—these fade even during the intervals of lovemaking;
like the beauty of moonlight, which becomes devoid of its charm when its excellence has passed, they no longer serve as objects for the eyes of those filled with desire. (VidSrk 13.5)

As her beloved, the lotus, approaches with its luster fading, the water sheds tears as if earned from the destruction of the lotuses— tears watched over by swans standing inside and outside day and night, their wings soiled and worn, who surround it like affectionate kinsmen.

For the fortunate, whose bodies are filled with manifold pleasures and delights from embracing dark-limbed women whose mouths are full of fresh betel nut, the arrival of the cold season is delightful;
but for us, whose knees are seized by trembling as we cover and uncover our chests with torn and patched cloths, the heart simply sinks.
The monkeys tremble violently; the cattle, goats, and sheep wither away from the scarcity of water; and the dog, though cast out for even a moment from the hollow of the hearth, does not leave it.

In this place,

36. Then, on the subject of majesty:

The Lord Viṣṇu bore the entire earth; the serpent bore him as well as that earth; and the ocean bore even him along with them.

What can we say of the ocean’s splendor? Having taken some drops of water from this ocean, the clouds then fill the earth, obstructing the sky with their waters;

Of Muñjarāja.

The sage who, having drunk this [ocean], dwells upon its shore bears an internal burning like that of a garland of fire; and he is that Aurva fire who, having been greatly harassed for the sake of all his kinsmen, now sleeps upon the lap of the glorious Hari. Salutations to that Agastya: by whom the ocean—the very limit of all great wonders—was thus drunk; for therein Hari, as the playful Boar, had repeatedly submerged himself, causing the delusion of being a whale, while Mount Meru was uprooted by his breath and spread across the expanse of the sky, yet even when drunk, his belly was not filled.

His birth was from Jamadagni; that blessed Lord Pinākin is his guru; and his renunciation is characterized by the unfeigned gift of the earth sealed by the seven oceans.

On this side dwells Keśava, and on that side his enemies; here rest the birds of the mountains who have come for refuge, and there is the submarine fire along with all the clouds of universal destruction—oh, how vast, powerful, and capable of bearing the weight is the form of the ocean!

Regarding Madhukūṭa:

Vallaṇa’s:

What shall we say of Hari? Is it that the entire universe is in his belly, or rather that he himself lies upon the hood of the serpent, who occupies but a single spot within the ocean? If the vastness of the ocean were not such as this, or if its profundity did not exist, or if its compassionate favor toward the realm of all sentient beings were not of such a kind; (of whom [could it be said]? By the powerful submarine fire, blazing within, consuming the waters, and emitting garlands of flames—who would not be reduced to nothing but ashes?

Victorious is that sage whose blazing fire digests within his belly the waters of the ocean, such that only the water remaining at the end of the sea has somehow been vomited up; moreover, from that very fire of his stomach, as if it were fresh, the submarine fire (*vāḍava*) has emerged again through the process of being vomited at that moment, having entered back into the waters for Yama. Of Dharmakīrti:

A disposition mostly pleasant, a restraint in speech sweet with modesty, a mind naturally auspicious, and an irreproachable acquaintance—whether before or after, this secret of the virtuous, whose essence is never distorted, remains pure and triumphant even without instruction. (VidSrk 37.2)
Whether those skilled in policy revile me or praise me, whether fortune descends upon me or departs as she pleases,
whether death comes this very day or at the end of an eon, the steadfast do not stir even a single step from the path of justice.

Of Tryambaka:
"When I was a knower of only a little, blinded by pride like an elephant in rut, my mind became arrogant, thinking, 'I am omniscient.

Like two needles in the first and last parts of Kālidāsa’s *Nītiśataka* (verse 8)— the wicked man and the good man respectively— one creates a hole, while the other fills it. (VidSrk 37.6) [1218]
Gobhaṭṭa:
The virtuous, who are like stalks of sugarcane from Puṇḍra—possessing sweet juice by nature—bow down as much as they wish of their own accord;

By Rājaśekhara:

Of Śrī Dharmadāsa:
The nature of the wicked here is indeed a mind of fault-finding toward those who recognize virtue, and an intellect impassioned with hatred toward those whose disposition is graceful and modest.
Both of these inevitably arise at all times; yet even one who is clever and self-controlled speaks only of his own fame. (VidSrk 38.50)
Thus ends the section on the non-existent. //38//

39. Then, at daybreak, the traveler sets out upon his wretched journey, his cheeks moistened by the trickling of teardrops; with a sluggish gait produced by somewhat bent shanks, his knees worn out and afflicted by old age; clutching his staff with his fist, his tattered garment slipping from his waist, his throat scorched and groaning, he rises and proceeds along the road, fainting from the harsh wind. VidSrk_39.1
A traveler, his desires fulfilled by merit, initially disregarding the fault of the burning heat, has slept through the night at the shrine of the village goddess upon a floor of long, thin grass.
Now trembling in his worn-out rag, cracked by the pounding of his feet, he moves from corner to corner with a moan as the wind blows fiercely, laden with icy droplets, shattering his slumber.
By Bāṇa (Svsu.ā. 1857). VidSrk_39.2. (1305)
O housewife,
you maintain these children by whatever means possible until the end of the summer months.
Afterwards, once the downpour from the clouds has arrived, the gourd and the pumpkin flourish; at that time, what are we kings? What are we? (VidSrk 39.3)
For Dharaṇīdhara:

My children, emaciated by hunger, are like corpses; my kinsmen show me little regard; and the leaking water from a cracked, worn-out pitcher does not trouble me so much as the needle when it is requested every day from my neighbor, who, having made a sarcastic smile, becomes angry as I try to mend my wife’s torn garment. (VidSrk 39.4)
Of someone:

With crying infants and leaf-cups [of food] before their father, the daughter-in-law hidden away, and the housewife standing in the middle skilled in dividing the portions—with whatever food has somehow been obtained as collateral for the cloth covering her hips, the offering of life-breaths is made while the sun is a circle red with vermilion. (VidSrk 39.5)

These children of the poor, placing their thin, worn, and soiled rags upon their shoulders, their limbs bristling with goosebumps, engage in quarreling during the cold season in order to secure a spot on a wall dappled by the shimmering rays of the sun. (VidSrk 39.6)
In that very same house is the kitchen, right there the mortar, right there the utensils, right there the children, and right there his own dwelling.

Even for such a man who has endured this as a householder in distress, what can we say of his miserable state, when tomorrow his wife, about to give birth, will be grinding [grain] in that very same place?
Of someone (Vainateya):
Thinking, "Today the meal for the young ones has been secured by my strength; but how will it come about tomorrow? she remained anxious.
Thus, with the regions of her cheeks stained by falling tears, the wife of a poor man does not wish for the end of the night.
Someone laments over the soaked barley meal; she wards off the weeping children by pouring water from a bowl; she protects the straw bedding.
Having placed a broken shard of a winnowing basket upon her head, the distressed housewife of a ruined home—what is there that she does not do when the god rains so heavily? (VidSrk 39.9)
Of Yogeśvara (Skmsa.u.ka. 2245, Laṅgadatta; Svsu.ā.
3201): "I am the sole author in the matter of binding the knot of my tattered garment."
The housewife of the hero Vīra, who had mastered the science of distributing limited and coarse food, said:

"Do not weep for long; come here, my child. Seeing that these other sons are of no avail today, your father will give you a necklace and two garments when he returns. (VidSrk_39.10; Skmsa.u.ka. 2230; Bhānu)
Having heard these words of his wife, the penniless traveler, sighing near the wall with his face bowed down by tears, departed once more on his journey. *VidSrk* 39.11 (1314).
"The *kūṣmāṇḍī* plant bears fruit incessantly when sprinkled with golden water"—this was said by many well-wishers, and we accepted it as such.

But having requested some from the house of a wealthy man and bringing it slowly, it has indeed dripped away drop by drop along the path itself into the interior of the earthen cooking pot. (VidSrk 39.12)
"Mother, devoted to righteousness, show mercy to me, a weary traveler from a foreign land; staying hidden in the corners of the porch near the door, I shall pass the night.
Thus rebuked by these words from the fierce face of his wife, the traveler, his only wealth now a handful of straw held in his hand, slowly departs.
Of a certain [person]—(Svsu.ā. 2416, ant spd śā.pa.
580 Ravidatta, Smvsū.mu.
96.3 Ravigupta).
(Śatānanda’s, Skmsa.u.ka. 1341):

A householder with his son is caught by the pair of horns; his two elderly parents are at the sides; his wife is at the tip of the tail; his children are clinging to the hooves; and his daughter-in-law is on the dewlap.
By the power of fate, this single worn-out old ox, who has become the very essence of everything in the home, is being roused from sleep while the entire family weeps. VidSrk_39.14 *(1317) //
For someone like me,
who am destitute of clothing, my very skin— adorned with sprouts of horripilation caused by the onset of cold winds— acts as a garment. (VidSrk 39.15)
The cage of a poor man's body would surely burst asunder this very instant,
were it not held fast and bound tightly by the ropes of his desires.

Generally, the children of the poor, their bodies pressed against the doorways of others' mansions with their sprout-like hands outstretched, desiring food while their words hidden by shame, alas, look upon the eater with but half an eye. (VidSrk 39.17)
O Creator, for whomsoever you have provided feet for the sake of travel-wearying, a wife for the sake of separation, speech for the sake of begging, and a body for the sake of old age—
if you feel no shame in always granting these things to me, do you at least not feel any exhaustion? (VidSrk 39.18)
In the mouth of the food-bowl, what does the belly-demon desire?
The penniless man, living in miserable poverty, agitates his wife. Better to be dead than base; yet even so, there is a vast difference between them.
No one among all people takes away the name of that single person who is a friend to men.
Let the miser have poverty, which brings about the veil of stinginess;
let his wealth be a drum skilled at proclaiming that very fault. (VidSrk 39.21)
Vyāsa:
Even while living, and even as a corpse, this wretch gives nothing;
by increasing his flesh, he has merely rendered a service to the crow.
Kavirāja says:
It is established that whatever is a *śrīphala* (the fruit of the bilva tree) is not long;
he who maintains an absolute conviction in this matter is considered truly simple-minded. VidSrk_39.23 *(1326)*
Between a miser and a sword— both of which have their fists tightly clenched, rest in a sheath, and are naturally dark— their difference lies solely in their outward form. (VidSrk 39.24)
Gobhaṭṭa:
O traveler, abandon this vain longing; you have surely not realized that you have arrived here too late.
This is a house of snakes, a den of serpents, the vicinity of which even crows do not approach. (VidSrk 39.25)
By him who created sleep for the eyes at the setting of the sun, why was death not ordained for mortals when their wealth is exhausted? (VidSrk 39.26)
By that very fragment of sky through which the sun travels by day, the moon travels by night; oh, the wretchedness of these two!
With our defiled bodies, we have approached every house;
like crows in our conduct, we are our own heralds. (VidSrk 39.28)
Therefore, my hope for the instruction on *bahuvrīhi* compounds has become utterly vain;
my mind is like that of one who is deluded by failing to perceive the connection between what precedes and what follows. (VidSrk 39.29)
Thus ends "The Wanderings of the Wretched. //39//
40. Next, a series of *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroborative applications):
Where is the search for that serpent submerged within the waters of the Yamunā—waters dark as fragments of crushed sapphire, resembling a mass of accumulated collyrium?

For if the circle of jewels upon his hoods were not radiant with star-like luster, he would not have attained such eminence; indeed, by those very qualities through which the virtuous achieve greatness, they also meet their downfall. (VidSrk 40.1)
With his hopes shattered, his body shriveled like a basket, and his senses withered by hunger, a rat made a hole and at night fell of its own accord into the mouth of a serpent.
Satiated by that creature's flesh, the serpent quickly departed by the very same path; remain at ease, for fate alone is turbulent in both the prosperity and the ruin of the world.

For whose sake kings, bound by mutual enmity, abandon even their dear lives like blades of grass—that very Earth drinks the blood of those she has slain; for Fortune, when enjoyed by many, generally undergoes a transformation.
The chariot has but a single wheel; its seven horses are restrained by serpents; the path is without support, and the charioteer is likewise footless.
Yet the Sun reaches the end of the boundless sky every day; for the great, success in action depends upon their inner strength, not upon external instruments.

How was it that Paulastya did not recognize the fault in abducting another’s wife? How was it that the son of Kakutstha did not perceive the impossibility of a golden deer? And how was it that Yudhiṣṭhira did not understand the great vice of dice? Generally, the intellect of those whose minds are deluded by approaching calamity comes to naught. (VidSrk 40.5)
Whether true or false, the rumor of people may at will rob even those of lofty station of their greatness;
for the sun, though its entire darkness has been clearly dispelled as it emerges from the scales, does not possess such brilliance when it has entered Virgo.
That the day is shortened at the onset of winter, and that the summer night is made briefer—
by this pair of examples, it is understood that Fate is intent upon the contraction of all good things.
The Ocean gave his daughter to the one clad in yellow robes (Viṣṇu), and the poison Kālakūṭa to the one clad in sky-clad rags (Śiva).
Tell me, which of these two possessed the superior quality? For generally, people show respect based merely on one's outward appearance.

Of what avail is birth in this world, or by whom is it observed? A man attains preeminence through his own power alone. For jars are not able to dry up even a well, yet the ocean itself was drunk by the one born from a jar (Agastya).
One should concern oneself only with defining the true nature of a man; talk regarding his birthplace, his virtues, or his faults is utterly in vain.
Who welcomes the *kālakūṭa* poison because it arose from the ocean, or who reviles the lotus because it was born from the mud? (VidSrk 40.10)
A bald man, scorched on his head by the rays of the sun, went to the foot of a *bilva* tree in search of shade, the enemy of the heat.
There too, his head was suddenly shattered by a *bilva* fruit falling at that very moment. Generally, wherever one devoid of fortune goes, there he becomes a vessel for calamities. (VidSrk 40.11)
His ornament is a hell-guardian who causes suspicion; his retinue is Bhṛṅgin with shattered limbs; and his wealth is a single, aged bull.
Such is the condition even of Sthāṇu, the teacher of the immortals, when the crooked Fate stands upon his head—what then are we? VidSrk_40.12 *(1344)
Those who are treasuries of courtesy do not here require the condition of kinship; for among those whose love is joyful, such [courtesy] arises as their very nature.
What indeed are these kinships? They are like the Malaya breezes and mango trees, for upon reaching them, one produces a gift of joy at every joint.
Noble birth does not establish a man in the world-transcending conduct; for high-mindedness has no cause other than character itself.
The sage who drank the vital breath of Vātāpi was born from a jar, yet his playful feat was the drinking of the ocean.
Chased by a mirage over parched ground, the thirsty deer does not cease, even though its body is exhausted;
not knowing the truth, it does not seek another lake, for hope placed in an impossible object bears no fruit and only creates an obstacle.
Does the tortoise feel no pain from the burden upon his body that he does not cast the earth down? Or is there no exhaustion for the sun-god that he does not remain motionless?
Rather, a praiseworthy person, like a miser, feels ashamed when abandoning what has been undertaken; indeed, the fulfillment of things once promised is, alas, the singular vow of the virtuous.
Some rare person is pure-hearted by nature; in this matter, association with the virtuous or noble birth is not the cause.
The Kālakūṭa poison, born from the Ocean of Milk and residing in the throat of Śiva, never abandons its own blackness. (VidSrk 40.17)

His garment is a hide, his ornament is a corpse’s head, his food is obtained by begging, and his only cow is unskilled even at plowing—understanding that such is the wealth of Śarva, the Ganges turns her face away from that abode of jewels; alas, how miserable is the life of one in such a wretched state, who is abandoned even by his wife!
Though released from the grasp of the fisherman’s rough hand, the wretched minnow fell back into the net;
by fate it escaped even that, only to be swallowed by a heron—tell me, when fortune is adverse, how can there be an end to calamity? (VidSrk 40.19)
He does not dig at the surface of the earth with his hooves, nor does he bellow loudly; seeing a person before him, he does not even become angry at a cow.
Yet, as a beast of burden, he bears the yoke with fortitude and without upraised neck. In this world, the wise excel others through the magnanimity of their actions. (VidSrk 40.20)
From the head of Śiva we have fallen to heaven; from the head of Paśupati to a mountain peak; from that lofty mountain to the surface of the earth; and from this earth to the ocean below.
Like the Gaṅgā descending ever downward, we have reached a great distance; or rather, for those who stumble from their footing, ruin takes on a hundred forms.
In this world, for some person, from somewhere, and for some reason, what does it matter whether mental states possess virtues or faults?
For the Ganges, disregarding the lofty mountain, flows toward the lowly ocean. (VidSrk 40.22)

Having been repeatedly deceived by mistaking the reflection of stars for lotuses, the discerning swan, searching for water-lily stalks during the nights, does not bite them again even by day, fearing they are stars; for a person startled by a trick suspects danger even when the truth is present. (VidSrk 40.23)
One who is obsessed with what is impossible is generally a fool, not a wise man;
for who other than a child would wish to grasp the shimmering reflection of the moon in water?
Even if they lack merit, the virtuous generally do not abandon one who has taken refuge in them with devotion.
The moon bears even its own spot, which shares in its waxing and waning.
(40.25) A base person constantly and excessively oppresses the virtuous, even though they remain unchanged;
what wrong has the lotus ever done to the frost that it always consumes it? (40.26)

That the Lord of the Bow was struck down by a mere child, that the son of Jamadagni caused the earth to be abandoned at his preceptor’s word, and that the ocean was bound—all these were achieved one by one by Rāma, the destroyer of the ten-necked Rāvaṇa; how can he be described? Describe fate instead, by which even he was suddenly reduced to being nothing but a story.
People bow to the moon when it has just risen as a mere crescent, but not to it once it is full; Hara bears the celestial river Gaṅgā upon his head, but not the daughter of the mountain (Pārvatī);
Hari, the lord of the three worlds, abandoned Lakṣmī for the sake of his beloved Gopikās; the world, hating its familiar virtues, desires ever what is new. (Vidagdha-śataka 40.28)
What wonder is there in this, that for those who desire the fruit of wealth from the seed of knowledge—which has tranquility as its fruit—the undertaking becomes fruitless?
For all things have fixed domains and do not undergo transformation; a grain of rice can never produce a sprout of javā.

The deer, afflicted by thirst, cried out repeatedly toward every cloud; the clouds, for their part, immediately released showers of water toward them again and again. What are the clouds to the birds here, or what are the birds to the rain-clouds? For those in distress there is nothing that cannot be asked for, and for the great there is nothing that cannot be used to help others. (VidSrk 40.30)
By Bhartṛhari:
Whether it be water, fire, wind, ether, earth, or even the entire universe itself— what is not easily accomplished for that Viṣṇu, the conqueror of the gods?
Even though Bali was led downward by the trickery of the dwarf-form, he nevertheless, by his very nature, fashioned even that [dwarf] into a wheel-turner with his own discus.
Is this moon not radiant? Does it not possess all its digits? Does it not grant joy to the eyes with its upward-pointing rays?
Yet, fallen into the maw of Rāhu, it has set. Truly, in the hearts of the wicked, virtues are like blades of grass. (VidSrk 40.32)
Of the incomparable [suffering]:
first the sesame seeds were harvested; thereafter they underwent drying; from drying they indeed attained purification, and then they reached heating;
from heating came the pressings of the most rigid machine—thus, oil is the cause of this succession of miseries. (VidSrk 40.33)

This milk-like affection which you have maintained is a cause of singular calamity, for its sake you have been exiled, further mutilated, uprooted, and cast into the fire. (VidSrk 40.34) The Supreme Lord bears upon his head the moon, which is crooked, dull-natured, and waning; yet at his ear he has placed the lord of serpents, who is expert in harming others.
The storehouse of virtues, Nandī, has been cast out at the gate; alas, what can be said here? A lord is generally unskilled in discerning between those who are worthy and unworthy recipients.

If the Ten-faced one had not abducted the wife of the descendant of Kakutstha, where would there be the ocean, where the construction of the bridge, and where the victory over Laṅkā after crossing it?
If the enemy had not brought about the defeat of Pārtha, where would such penance be? For generally, those who possess self-respect are led by their enemies to the highest state of eminence.
It is said that conch shells, having emerged from the ocean, are burned by forest fires on its shores; yet they become jewels upon the palms of merchants' hands and reach the crowns of kings.

Displacement from one's place leads to ruin for the petty, but the virtuous, always carrying their qualities with them as they travel to foreign lands, attain ever higher and praiseworthy eminence. (VidSrk 40.37)

Alas, that one who is the supreme friend of the worlds, the producer of bliss, the possessor of all arts, the glorious one, the auspicious jar at the time of lovemaking, the source of nectar, and the crest-jewel upon the head of the Destroyer of Tripura—he now goes to his setting; indeed, the courses of destiny are inherently treacherous.
"This is a fruitless despondency, thinking 'we have escaped our enemies'; rather, it is proper to constantly devise a remedy against them.
Did not the enemy of the Dānavas, though defeated by Jarāsaṃdha along with the wielder of the plow, later slay him with his dear friend, the son of the Wind?"
The moon wanes, its form is naturally crooked, it is cold-natured, and it appears as a fault at the time of the sun’s decline;
yet it is borne upon the head by the Supreme Lord. For the great, there is no consideration of merits or faults regarding those who have sought their protection.
The moon whitens the soiled quarters of the sky, yet it does not whiten the stain residing within itself;
for those whose minds are ever intent on accomplishing what is right, great beings never exert themselves for their own selfish ends. (VidSrk 40.41)
The wise man accepts what is right and abandons the rest; this is the innate discernment of the great.
Even when milk and water are mixed together, the royal swan separates them, drinking the pure milk and leaving the water behind. (VidSrk 40.42)

Generally, for one who dwells in an unsuitable place, the highest good is merely the preservation of one's own life. What thought can there be of blossoming for a *campaka* tree whose roots are being scorched by the burning sands of a desert within? (VidSrk 40.43)
Through knowledge—even though his body is swallowed by the planets, the sun here still awakens the clusters of lotuses;
for the great, once they have undertaken a task, fulfill it even in the face of adversity. (VidSrk 40.44)
Even great gain obtained through prostration does not lead to happiness for the wise man;
the cātaka bird, though possessing a neck of infinite length, takes only a tiny amount of water.
Whose mind finds delight in wealth merely by its utility? Who does not tremble when standing upon a support no larger than one's own foot? (VidSrk 40.46) [1378]
Behold this cloud: it approaches the salt ocean, endures the onset of many winds, and experiences various breakers before it;
yet, having somehow obtained its waters, it bestows them upon the world. Its addiction to giving does not calculate whether there is merit or fault in it. *Vidvatsamvādaśataka* 40.47. (1379)
Of Vallaṇa:
(Srkm 1943) The sun diminishes the luster of the moon, the abode of nectar; he plunders the host of stars and scatters his hot radiance; he quells the beauty of the night-lotus groves.
The sun knows very well that every day he must fall upon the western mountain, yet being restless with his fresh rising, what does he not do? VidSrk_40.48 (1380)
Of Kavirāja—thus ends the section on Arthāntaranyāsa (Corroboration by a General Truth). //40//

41. Furthermore, O King, at the time of your victorious expedition, as the mass of dust from the earth—spreading forth from the hooves of the rows of Kamboja horses—kissed the sky, the horses of the sun experienced the pleasure of rubbing their limbs against it; moreover, they found kinship with the lotuses in the celestial river [the Gaṅgā] in the vault of heaven. VidSrk_41.1 *(1381) //
Of someone (Vasukalpa):
When your machines set forth, the sky is filled with floods of vermilion from the frontal globes of herds of rutting elephants, scattered by the flapping of their constantly moving ears.

Bearing the luster of the flowers of the *pāribhadra* tree, the rays of the Lord of Days, though it was midday, caused the *cakravāka* birds to look upon them with eyes startled by the illusion that it was the twilight of sunset. O Warrior in Battle! Your sword—victorious in its splendor, long as the glance of Śrī, glossy and dark, and beautiful as a blue water-lily—weighs like a sapphire placed in milk during this year when the milk is the white flood of the fame of rival kings, as it undergoes its trial.
The elephants of the quarters, repeatedly taking up the ink of rut from their temples with the pens of their own trunk-tips,
O illustrious Candradeva, inscribe praises of your victory upon the inner leaves of the *tāḍī* palms on the shores of the ocean.
— By Abhinanda.

Red with passion for the virtuous, black as death to your enemies, and yellowed by the glances of women’s eyes—you are white with fame; thus it is true that you encompass the four castes and the four stages of life.
O Immovable One—
you do not produce joy in Kaṃsa, you bear a body graced by Yaśodā,
and you do not abandon your orientation toward the Truth; thus it is true that you are Vāsudeva.
O Bhadra—there is no elision of letters, nor indeed is there the application of suffixes after [a preceding element], nor is there any modification anywhere, nor are the original bases ever broken;
whether it be *guṇa* or *vṛddhi*, your rule of word-formation is more capable than even that of the Sage, the son of Dakṣī, for the constant benefit of the world. (VidSrk 41.7)
From Pāṇini (Skmsa.u.ka.
1378, Śabdārṇava): It is true that Nārada gladdens Indra by proclaiming your virtues; however, the bees buzzing around his garlands of *pārijāta* flowers hum with a sound harsh to the ear.
If they are warded off by a host of Apsarases with the grand display of yak-tail whisks, then the jingling sound of the bracelets on their undulating vine-like arms will become unbearable.
Of Madhukūṭa—the island of whom was the earth and the ocean was his mouthful of water; though he was a singular marvel, even his body became difficult to perceive in the sky when swallowed by you.
The three worlds were drunk by him, and those [worlds] were drunk for the sake of rest by Viṣṇu (Kaiṭabhāri); and he [Viṣṇu] is within your heart. You alone are to be saluted.
Of the servant of the Tathāgata: (Skmsa.u.ka.

1377) Those impoverished Vedic scholars whose courtyards were once filled with heaps of cotton seeds and whose small huts were surrounded by walls of woven reeds—now, by your grace, pearls from the necklaces of young women, loosened during games and sports, fall upon the grounds surrounding their palatial mansions. VidSrk_41.10 *(1390) //

Victorious for a long time are the dust-particles of your lotus-feet, which are like a powder for subduing Fortune (Lakṣmī) herself— the very ones that, when joined to the foreheads of men by prostration, erase the ill-fated letters written there by destiny. (VidSrk 41.11)
Of Abhinanda:
"O Lord, if you are the moon, the treasury of digits, then we are the oceans; and if you are the lord of waters, the treasury of boundaries, then we are the clouds."
If you are a cloud that fulfills all hopes, we are the trees; if you are beautiful by abiding on the path of the virtuous, we are the travelers. (VidSrk_41.12, Dakṣa’s; Skmsa.u.ka.
1437, by someone) [We are like] snakes devoid of power, dwelling in holes, their coils contracted in fear.
Your name, sung by the forest-dwellers, torments your enemies like a syllable of a mantra.
(VidSrk_41.13) By him alone.
O Lord of Men, those houses in which the harsh sound of conchs, potsherds, and moving adzes was formerly heard, now—through your favor—[are filled with the sound of Vedic recitation].
The sweet-sounding resonance of the lute is heard, enriched by the tinkling of rows of bracelets slipping from hands whose fingers move in the rhythmic sequence of the six *jātis*.
To someone [Bhāsa]:
O Lord, I entreat you; be gracious and abandon this undertaking of war.
At present, the only rivals who possess such loftiness are the mountains.
O King, let it be that you are praised by yourself; indeed, all the sacred scriptures dwell within our hearts. Yet, nowhere else is there a true ford like this one: namely, the edge of your sword.

Desiring to purify his own body, a single enemy received it upon his head; through its twofold nature [coolness and sharpness], he instantly attained first the state of the twice-born (brahminhood), then the state of the five elements (death), and finally the state of the thirty-three gods (heaven).
O Lord of the Discus,
to you who have conquered the earth as far as my very self, pearls and other gems were indeed already offered by me; now I have become destitute of all possessions.
O King, at dawn, this ocean before you bears a heated axe in the guise of the rising solar disc, its arms being the waves tossed upward.
O King, may you be the conqueror of the lands of the nine divisions of the earth, as was foretold by the clusters of trees in the desert; for through your grace, we [shall attain our goal].

O illustrious Muñja, we rejoice, for the ground is slippery with the mud of the floating tears trickling from the channels of the eyes of the wives of the merchant-fleeters who have recently perished. VidSrk_41.18 (1398)

In the winter, out of fear of the wind cold with frost, your enemies lie embracing their own slender bodies with both arms—bodies that are like beloved women who have cast off their ornaments, whose voices are soft, who emit sighs, who tremble, whose lips are wounded, who are unclothed, and who bear a thrill of horripilation; they embrace them with excessive passion as if they were their own forms. (VidSrk 41.19)
Soiled by contact with the earth and falling dust, fallen from their own homes, fearlessly embraced in the palms of even common folk,
sometimes stuck together, sometimes bound and then released— your enemies' wives have wandered from house to house like the pieces on a game of dice.

In your enemy’s empty city, the innocent wife of a hunter now longingly intends to seize—with a meaningful look—the serpent, dark as soot, who stands with his two hands and feet stiffened and helpless, having been gripped by the head of a frog whose essence of nourishment was stored during the rains; she mistakes him for a golden-tipped arrow held in her fist.
O Cittapa,
you have not loosened your cross-legged posture, nor have you risen from your lion-throne; nor has the creeper of your brow been raised like a column of smoke from the fire of your wrath.
O Śrīcandra, the splendors of the crest-jewels of kings—jewels that emit dense clusters of shimmering and beautiful rays—now blossom at your lotus-like feet. VidSrk_41.22 *(1402) //

O King, in the palace of your enemies, the state of governance remains exactly as it was even though their long-standing beloveds are gone: the gates are guarded by swordsmen and outside by elephants with rut-fluid trickling from their temples; the inner floors are occupied by chamberlains wearing shimmering jewels; and the couches are occupied solely by the queens. (Vidyākara’s Subhāṣitaratnakośa 41.23)
Of Vijayapāla.
